paragraphs.text: Bright and splendid is the celebration of the present feast, yet it shines out brighter still through the zeal of those who have hurried together to it. It has its evident magnificence in itself, but it makes that magnificence public through the gathering of those who assemble. It is made radiant by the multitude, and it makes the multitude radiant by the shining of its graces. It does not gain an increase of light by taking a share in anything else. Rather, by sharing out its own brightness and making it plain and visible to those gathered, it spreads out along with the splendour of its radiance. This visible sun keeps its utmost brightness within itself even when it is hidden from our eyes. But when it rises and peers out from the lofty mountains, it spreads its rays over the loveliest things in creation, and by lighting them up it heightens the grandeur of the marvel. In the same way today's feast, made resplendent by the spiritual light of grace, has its ever-shining brightness in itself, but it extends that brightness through the gathering, in due proportion, of those who run together and are enlightened. Since, then, this feast shines with the mystical rays of the Spirit, and all who come together at it are enlightened, it would be better than anything else one could choose to run to it eagerly and be enlightened: to have our minds illumined and to be bathed in light, not veiled by the perishable cloud. For such is the brightness of joy spread over the present feast, and so it imparts a radiance more lasting than visible things, or rather far brighter than they.

For today, as the spiritual cloud is proclaimed to be spreading out, the rays of the light that never sets begin to rise upon the world, and the darkness of godlessness that had prevailed begins to wane and be driven off. Today, as the building of the divine tabernacle is announced, the foundations of godliness are laid, and the strongholds of impiety are shaken from their base. Today, as the royal purple is being woven, the coming of the King of all is announced in advance; the reconciliation of a humanity at war is sketched out beforehand; the trophies over their enemy are proclaimed ahead of time. Today the root of good things, foretold to spring up in a barren womb, announces that it will make our nature, withered by wickedness, put forth fresh shoots of godliness. Today the King's gate, through which no one may pass, is set firmly in place and made ready for his passage, which is beyond understanding, and it makes the gates of heaven passable for us. Today childless parents, given the good news that they will bring forth the cause of the abundant fruitfulness of good things, prepare for the whole human race a share in that wealth. How glorious is their memory, reaching through all the ages! How their fame endures, never to be taken from them! How blessed was their election, and how worthy of blessing their excellence in virtue, through which they also came to be chosen! For in this they surpassed all their kind by the nobility of their choice, and so they rose above them by the magnificence of the gifts bestowed on them in their election. They were honoured above the whole race, because they honoured the Creator of all things above all. They were preferred, because they preferred the love of the Master to their own lives. They were chosen in advance for the ministry of mysteries, because they chose at all times to fulfil only the will of the one who chose them. They were glorified, because they glorified him by their own deeds. They were magnified by the munificence of grace, because they made themselves worthy beforehand to receive it. This is what honoured them above all the righteous who had gone before. This [?] them of the

mysteries; this caused the fulfilment of what had been prophesied to them and long desired and sought to begin to come about. For this reason they were set above all their fellow tribesmen and obtained an incomparable dignity. For they kept the royal lineage unmixed, and by their royal virtues they preserved it unadulterated and free of counterfeit. They were not dragged down from the height of their dignity to the slavish abasement of pleasures. Instead, they kept its magnificence undiminished and were celebrated with a proclamation befitting it; and the Queen of all, as godly [?]

[?] and of might they were counted worthy to bring forth as fruit. For the history that tells their story, setting it out in harmony with the facts, says this: just as they preserved their godlike beauty and their original comeliness, so too they kept the nobility of their race unmixed. They were honoured among the finest of the tribes, or rather they surpassed those who were honoured. They were rich in abundance of outward goods, but richer still in the generosity of their choice. Wealth summons others to pleasures and drags them down, but they made it the material of goodness and a stepping-stone to the heights of virtue. They not only fulfilled what was required by law and ordinance, by which blessing is assigned to wealth and good order to those who bring offerings, but in many things the voice [?], a proof of what is recorded in secret [?]

going beyond these, or rather dedicating the whole of their wealth to God, they surpassed all who brought offerings by the magnanimity of what they offered. For, it says, Joachim offered his gifts twofold, saying: “What comes from my abundance shall be for all the people, and what is for my forgiveness shall be for the Lord God.” O these acceptable gifts! O offering laid up in treasuries no thief can plunder! O wealth that stored up the inexhaustible abundance of good things! O choice admired for the lavishness of its offerings! Just as, he says, it is right to offer to God what is prescribed by the ordinances, so it is fitting to set the whole of one's abundance before the people and the needy. For these things too are offered to God through those who receive them. And what law, O righteous man, commands bringing gifts and offerings twofold? What ordinance prescribes distributing all one's abundance to the people? No law, he says, and no ordinance compels anyone to do these things. Rather, he discovered the good by himself, as something God would choose, and he fulfils it. “The wealth that was given,” he says, “is his, and it is right to give it back to him. Since these things are benefits of his providence, let them benefit our kinsfolk in return. What has been given is abundance; let it be poured out on a people that is his own abundant possession. Since these things are grace and not rewards for works, let the facts confirm the name and proclaim the loving-kindness of the giver. Let the cares of wealth be shared among many, or rather let its whole burden be lifted from us. Let the crowd of possessions be scattered from the senses, so that they may lay hold of divine gifts unhindered. Let the cloud of cares that darkens the mind be driven away, so that it may gaze purely at the light of dispassion alone. Let not the wing of the mind be dragged down from its high-soaring tracks by the weight of perishable thoughts; let it complete its flight toward immaterial things unhindered. Let the ears of the soul remain undinned by the clamour of vain things and take in the voice of those who keep festival immaterially; let them catch the sweet melody of those who rejoice in heaven.” In this way the offering of the righteous, brought by so noble a mind, is deemed worthy of a fitting acceptance by the God of all. But those of his race who shared with the righteous man in bringing offerings at the solemn feasts did not admire the ardour of his God-loving magnanimity. Instead they envied its excess and put forward certain customs forbidding him to bring offerings to God, since he was childless and fruitless and deprived of anyone to carry on his line. “It is not lawful for you,” it says, “to offer your gifts, because you have not raised up offspring in Israel.” Some say it means, “It is not lawful for you to offer first”; others take it as

meaning that he was barred altogether from offering sacrifice. Whichever way it is taken, these are the injunctions of envious men. They ought to have admired the righteous man's munificence; they ought to have applauded the abundance of his offerings and rejoiced at the magnificence of his choice. But not only were they unwilling to consider the offerings worthy of a just acceptance; they even tried to send them away. You who wish to thrust them away, what fault did you find in the offerings that you put forward as a pretext for refusing them? What meanness did you detect in the one dedicating them? What did you discover in the offerings that was unwelcome? Are they not whole? Are they not admired not only because nothing is lacking but also because they are abundant? Were they not chosen and dedicated with a right intention? “But custom,” he says, “having prevailed with the firmness of law, [?] the childless

[?] to God. For, it says, ‘A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.’” And that offerings are made acceptable by these things, God himself, who receives them, will testify to you, and all who cast their vote with the better side would agree. Divine Scripture relates that God praised and accepted many sacrifices of the saints and the righteous, and the glory of those who offered them bears witness to it as well. Take Abel himself, the first righteous man to receive God's testimony. His gifts were praised and accepted not because he had children, but because of the lavish fruitfulness of his choice: because he dedicated the best things to God, and because he offered a sincere sacrifice unmixed with mean thoughts. Cain, too, offered a sacrifice while childless, and it was rejected not for childlessness but for the fruitlessness of his choice: for his barren meanness and self-loving preference, and for an unequal, or rather unjust, division that fell far short of what is fit to offer to God. So the Master approves the gifts justly offered by the righteous man, and as the plainest

sign of his acceptance he sends fire down from above, which consumes the offerings entirely and by this bright token proclaims the righteousness of the one who offered them. But the man who was shown to be unjust in dividing his offerings rightly fails to win acceptance. For he sees that the most just God not only does not approve them, but even reproaches him and openly exposes the wrongness of what he did. For God says to him: “You would not offer rightly if you did not divide rightly.” “You, Cain,” he says, “think it reasonable that your offering should be accepted, and you are vexed that it is disregarded and sent away. But since it was not fittingly divided, it was not rightly offered either. For you would not offer rightly if you did not divide rightly.” Some say this was said about the victims that were to be burnt whole. The ancients, they say, first cut the sacrifices they brought in two and divided them into portions, but Cain did not divide his offerings properly and therefore missed the mark. But this is far from the truth of Scripture. For Scripture says that Cain's offering was not an animal sacrifice but firstfruits of the produce of his hands: “Abel became a shepherd of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. And Cain brought from the fruits of the ground a sacrifice to God, and Abel too brought from the firstborn of his sheep and of their fat.” What, then, does “You would not offer rightly if you did not divide rightly” mean? What he is saying is this: “You will not be able to offer rightly unless you first divide rightly.” And what is dividing rightly? It is apportioning properly: the one who divides and selects what is offered to God must not allot the best to his own share and the worst to Him. Suppose people have common goods to divide. They choose and prefer someone able to divide them fairly, and they reject and dismiss anyone who strays from fairness in the portions. How then could the God of all, when Cain divided His own gifts unequally and unjustly, have accepted them without examination, or looked with favour on his gifts? “All things are mine, Cain,” he says. “These are the gifts of my care, the benefits of my compassion. I made you a sharer in them, not as a reward for works, but solely out of loving-kindness. I have no need of them, but I desire your salvation, and so I accept firstfruits. I do not command you to divide what has been given you into equal quantities; I am seeking, through the firstfruits, the God-loving disposition of your mind. I granted you to enjoy my good things and put you in charge of dividing what is offered to me, and I found you wicked toward your benefactor, ungrateful for the abundance of good things, malicious in dividing the firstfruits. In making that division you made it unworthy of the giver. For yourself

you picked out [?] of the gifts, and me you insulted with the meanness of your offering.” We have not said these things in passing, but because we wished to show that the selection and acceptance of offerings depend on a God-loving choice that abounds in the fruits of the virtues, rather than on having children. Nor should we be blamed for passing over, since our discourse aims at due proportion, how the patriarch Abraham, before he had the children through whom he showed that what was promised was truly fulfilled, built an altar, and how he was afterwards commanded to make that famous sacrifice. “Take for me,” it says, “a heifer three years old and a ram three years old,” and he is told to gather all the other things needed to prepare the whole burnt offering. Or for passing over the offerings of the other righteous made while they were childless, and the sacrifice of Manoah, which he was commanded to perform on the rock. Through it he and his barren wife received the good news that their childlessness would be ended, and as confirmation that what was announced would come to pass, they saw the angel who stepped into the flame and flew up to heaven. And as for the prophetess's offerings, acceptable in deed and word, how is it that you who quarrel over these things do not send them away? What offspring could you point to from the loins of Elijah and Elisha? Yet they continually offered acceptable spiritual sacrifices to God, and blood sacrifices as well when the occasion called for them. Why do you not also bar the childless and shut them out from the [?] hymns and the unceasing doxologies of God? For God approves these, when they are offered from a contrite soul, more than animal sacrifices. But you close the eyes of your mind and willingly bring on yourself blindness to what is good. Swollen with envy of the righteous man, you spew your venom at him, using the law as a pretext. “It is not lawful for you,” he says, “to offer the gifts.” Why? Because of the burning ardour of his [?]? Because of the [?] of his offerings? Because he fulfils God's law beyond what it requires and generously does good to you? For he himself says, “What comes from my abundance shall be for all the people.” So it is for you too, since you belong to his kindred people. Should you not have honoured his unrestrained love for the Creator and welcomed the grace he bestowed on the multitude? Should you not have admired his magnanimity, praised it, and repaid it with fitting thanks? Instead you are weighed down by the multitude of his surpassing merits, or rather by your envy of them, and you are borne down to the ground. Bent over, you cannot gaze at the light of his brilliant achievements. But he is lifted higher than your taunts and [?] treads the air [?]. He is not dragged down by them to the abasement of grovelling thoughts; he is not brought down from the height of magnanimity to the depth of despondency; he does not resist the reproaches; he does not fight against the

rebuke; he does not repel the unreasonableness of your malice with reasonable explanations. Instead, through his intimacy with God he shows that his offerings are acceptable and your rebukes unjust. He entrusts the ending of his childlessness to prayer, and when he obtains it he exchanges your reproaches for praise. For a little later you will see the munificent glory of his blessed offspring. You will see the boast exalted among his forefathers, the good fortune of nature, the fruit of prayers, the blessing of the form of humanity, the abundant wealth, the unending joy, and the provider of true gladness. So the righteous man, with nobility of mind toward those who rebuked him, bade farewell to all who were present and stripped for superhuman contests and the toilsome wilderness. He took no thought for returning home, nor did he first tell anyone at home what he intended. Anyone who considers this carefully would find it extraordinary and above the weaknesses of nature. For what might someone, setting aside his admiration for the man's love of God, say to him about his disregard for everything else? “Most admirable man, what is this that you plan, going beyond the righteous who came before you? With what thought are you putting your will into action? What could it be that divided your [?]? What [?] your union with your wife, the partner of your life? Did not the one who joined her to you as into one flesh also unite you in the same counsel? Just as you had to keep the bond of unity with her unbroken, should you not also have seen to it that your oneness of mind was kept intact? Should you not have anointed her for the same toils and secured for her a share in your labours, as in your fruit? But even if for these reasons you do not care to go back, you ought to have done so to spare her heavier griefs, to avoid causing her pain by the uncertainty of your journey, and to avoid tormenting her, through not knowing where you had gone, with countless wearing thoughts. You also ought to have set your household affairs in good order before setting out for what you longed for. Or do you not care for your abundant wealth, nor give any thought to your possessions, as though you had no attachment to visible goods and were not held by the compelling force of pleasant things?” “Yes,” says the righteous man, “none of these things can cut me off from converse with God: not the unity of nature, not the bond of kinsfolk, not abundance of wealth, not the company of friends. Nothing among the delights that are seen could draw me away from my longing for the goods that are unseen. Before me lies a contest of toilsome supplications, which calls me out alone and stripped to wrestle. Let everything that blocks the course be dismissed. Let nothing of present things stand in the way or hold back the intensity of my eagerness. The gifts given by God, let them be left to God to look after.

I know, then, that my wife Anna is of the same character and the same mind, and remains so even when she is not with me. I know, too, her unrestrained love for the Master, through which she serves his providence and supports my contests with labours of her own. She will not be torn from the bond of our union, any more than from our relationship. She will keep a wife's oneness of mind, just as she keeps her love of God unbroken. She will help more by her prayers when absent than when present. She will not fail to have her petition heard, for she will offer her prayers with a warmer faith. She brings them to God from a contrite soul. Out of her innate humility she will raise them up to the Benefactor, who alone is exalted and surpasses all understanding. For he is supremely good, and he listens to those who call upon him in truth.” Such are the merits of the righteous, which rise above nature; such is the overflowing wealth of their virtues; such is the ardour of their faith; such is their close intimacy with God. So they obtain what they seek beyond all hope; so they are told by divine oracle that they will bear as fruit their own blessing and the gladness of the world. For angels announced in advance that joy and gladness would accompany creation at her coming forth. Such, then, were your proclamations and wonders at the very beginning. And you, O Theotokos, who were foretold to spring from such parents, received an entrance into life that matched what had been announced. For it was fitting that you should be foretold by such voices; fitting that your great deeds should be announced in advance in such words; it was right that you should be signified beforehand by such symbols, [?] from such a root, and that you should come forth from such fruitful parents. It was fitting that from such a root such a shoot should spring up; fitting that you, the royal rod, should rise from royal plantings; fitting that from abundant virtues you, the abundant wealth of good things, should overflow; fitting that you should be called the daughter of such parents, and that they should be shown to be the parents of such a daughter. And just as you were chosen in advance out of all creation to be the Mother of God, so they were foreordained to be honoured as your parents above all who have ever had children. How surpassingly glorious, then, is the greatness of such providence! How far beyond all hymns are the wonders of the providence of the Master of all! How much more desirable than anything longed for are the good things that came about through you! How blessed in their delight are those who have been found worthy to enjoy them! For this alone could rightly be called enjoyment; this is a delight that never runs out, namely, delight in your wonders. Through it we are led by the hand to the unending feast, and through the joy you give us here we greet in advance the gladness to come. Through the gifts you now bestow we have the pledge of the good things that abide. Through the present celebration of your glory we hear the sound of those who rejoice for ever. Our boast because of you never disappoints [?].

…our hopes are secure, and the good things we wait for are already in our hands. For this reason we long to hold more gatherings in your honour, or rather to hold them without end, so that we may always share in the things we desire. Today, Lady [?], we celebrate the feast kept in your honour. We do not keep it as a feast discovered later. It is counted among the illustrious feasts, or rather it comes first in substance as it comes first in order. And so we enjoy the gladness it proclaims, we delight in its mystical banquet, and we are filled with the gifts it foretold. Through the joy it brings we store up eternal grace in advance, and we sing together with the choir of those who keep the feast in heaven. [?] You prepare us to be numbered with them and to share their feast; intercede for us, then, that with a voice of rejoicing we may offer unceasing praise in Christ himself, your Son and our God, the only gladness and joy of those who long for you. For to him belong honour, might and praise, with the Father [?] and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages.

An Encomium on the Conception of Saint Anne, Mother of the All-Holy Theotokos. To those who love God, nothing could seem sweeter or more delightful than this present gathering, not even the things that usually give a seeming pleasure through the senses. Such people put all their effort into what truly is and endures, not into what only seems good. The delights of this occasion last. They are sweet, and they lead up to the one thing truly desirable. Only those who prefer them and despise everything else would seek them. I see that you have made this choice and are eager to carry it out. You always choose the better things, and above all in this present gladness, where we can enjoy the pure goods through its delights. These delights lead us by the hand toward those goods, and what is done on earth goes before what is stored up in heaven. This is why the present brightness has been set before us, and why the whole mystery of God's loving plan for us came about. Through the wonders revealed in this present life, the eternal glory of things unseen is unveiled. Through new things done in the world, the renewal of humanity, which is beyond this world, is brought about. Through God's good pleasure here below, the joy of those above is won for our earthly nature. Through God, who was seen on earth, rest in heaven is made ready for mortals. This is why we have gathered. This is the gain stored up today for all who have assembled here. This is the cause both of the wonders now displayed and of the gathering held because of them.

For through the display of wonders, the most wonderful mystery of all, the salvation of our race, is unveiled. Our nature had been dried up by wickedness. Because of this, the barren woman, dead to childbearing, is rekindled to life, and the virgin birth, beyond nature, is newly brought about. See how displays of wonders lead the way for the paradox of God's plan. The renewal of the barren woman goes before the virgin's conceiving. The sprouting of one who could not bear goes before a birth beyond reason. Childbearing beyond hope goes before a pregnancy beyond thought. Through unexpected things, nature grows used to not disbelieving what is newly done beyond nature. From a barren woman a Virgin is born; from a Virgin, God is born in the body; and through both a new creation is brought about. This is what the present gladness announced to us beforehand. It confirmed this in advance by the wonder done for the righteous couple. Their child, born beyond hope, proclaimed it, and has been set before us as the beginning both of the ineffable mysteries and of their fulfilment. Today's feast, then, leads all the more illustrious feasts by the wonders accomplished in it. It is like a base and foundation laid beneath them, and like a foundation it gathers under itself all the mysteries that God has accomplished in various ways. So we must give it reverence and great joy, as the beginning and cause of all good things. We must honour the first steps of salvation. We must rejoice in the gladness of the righteous couple and join in their song of thanksgiving. Or rather, we must take all of it as our own, since these are our own benefits and the only true ones, and offer it back to our Benefactor. This thanksgiving should be offered through us rather than through others [?], since it is we, more than those who brought the feast about, who enjoy its gifts. But enough of this. We have gathered at the banquet of the righteous couple who invited us, and it is time to feast on their surpassing virtues. First let us set out what the previous discourse passed over, and then enjoy the sweetest things that come from them. That discourse brought forward Joachim's surpassing virtues and unfolded them as far as it could. It told how the envy of his fellow tribesmen kept him from bringing his generous gifts as he offered sacrifice. It told how he found one escape from the reproaches of others, which was to take refuge in God. It told of his superhuman endurance on the mountain and his prolonged fast, or rather, one might say, his fleshlessness. For he was so detached from bodily ties and kept a fast so foreign to nature that one could almost call him fleshless. The discourse recalled these things briefly, up to the message that came to him through an angel. But it left what followed unexamined, along with everything concerning chaste and righteous Anne. This was not because a full account of her had been lacking (we have explained these things elsewhere, as far as we were able),

but because they had not been treated at all [?] in a way that suits the present gladness and this God-loving gathering. So today we must first go through what concerns her, and only then unfold the rest of the subject and add it for those who have gathered. A little earlier we held Joachim in surpassing admiration, a man both generous and burning with love for God. We admired how he made no reply to the idle taunts of the Jews. He did not silence the arrogant boasting of those who reproached him by showing that no law had been broken in his offerings, or that the baseless charge against him had been invented out of envy. And we admired how he despised both these taunts and all his affairs at home, entrusted the whole matter to God alone, and showed superhuman endurance in the desert. As we then unfolded the righteous man's virtues and marvelled at how they excelled, so now, if we bring forward the achievements of his wife Anne, let us praise them with an equal wonder. For she too is glorified for her patience and endurance, equally with him, or rather surpassingly. Many facts show this and bring it before the eyes of anyone who wishes to see. There were the reproaches of her people over her childlessness, and the unexplained absence of her husband. Besides these, there were the bold taunts of her maidservant, and the curses her fellow tribesmen uttered over her childlessness. The maid brought these curses before her eyes, and by reminding her of them shot sharper arrows at the righteous woman. All these things would confirm it. But Anne set her endurance against the troubles that fell upon her. She suffered, for she was not insensible to them. Yet she was not thrown down from the height of patience, either into the low place of despair or into anger at those who attacked her. So she did not answer back those who reproached her, nor did she resist their unjust rebuke. She did not say that the lawbreaking they used as a pretext came from envy. She did not reproach them that this so-called crime was their own invention and was not written in the Scriptures. Nor [?] did she, proud of her noble lineage and supported by her sincere life, stand against them boldly and expose how rash and unreasonable their undertaking was. In the same way, when the partner of her virtue and of her whole life disappeared, she did not go about looking for him or call together all her acquaintances for the search. She did not search the mountains and unlikely places. She did not stir up a great commotion among her kin or loudly condemn the one who had gone away. She did not accuse him of planning something foreign to their partnership and life together, or of showing a disposition foreign to his former kindness, or of breaking a natural union. She did not accuse him of disregarding the law that had joined them and of neglecting all their affairs at home. None of these things wounded Anne's mind, for it could not be wounded. As for the reproaches, since they

did not touch her soul, she despised them. Her husband's absence did grieve her, since she was deprived of his goodness. But she believed that a higher providence had arranged it. So, mourning in prayer, she asked for him to reappear, and she begged God, the giver of good things, for a child. And why should we even marvel at her generous spirit in these matters? See how she responded to her maidservant's reproaches. She felt nothing petty, and she held back the just anger she might have felt toward the girl. She did not use the full severity of a mistress's authority against so frenzied a rebuke, nor did she [?] become angry at the boldness of those who behaved this way…

For what reasonable excuse did the girl have when she poured out these senseless taunts on her? Was it that at a time of prayer and a broken heart Anne did not copy the ways of the proud and haughty? Was it that she raised her petition to the Master with a lowly and humble bearing, just as her mind was lowly and humble? Was it that she would not accept the garment that pampered women prize? Was it that she pushed away, when it was brought to her at an unfitting time, the kind of adornment she had refused all her chaste life long? Someone may ask what this was, and what the headband in the story was, which Anne pushed away and sent back when it was offered to her. Some say it was a splendid bridal diadem, the kind women wore when they relaxed at festivities. It is likely that it was brought to Anne with some malice. Those who meant her harm thought it would slacken the intensity of her prayer. They thought that this untimely pleasure would distract her mind and lead her to dare something foreign to her chastity, and that God would then overlook her. That is why the girl who offered it, trying to remove any suspicion, said she had received it not from others but from the woman who had made it, who had given it purely as a kindness and for none of the purposes suspected. The phrase "the mistress of the work" shows this. But Anne sent the gift away as something that would lead to wrongdoing. She did so not only because of the malice she suspected, but also because she had never taken pleasure in wearing such ornaments. "I did not adorn myself like this even in the bloom of youth," she says. "In times of good cheer and of what people consider enjoyment, I took no delight in diadems woven like this. My reputation as one of a most royal lineage did not lift my thoughts to such things. My abundant wealth did not draw me into excessive care for my body." And see Anne's humility. Far from being proud of her achievement, she even declares herself guilty. "For even though I have not done this," she says,

"I see that I am paying the debts of some failings I do not know of. The Master, who examines hidden things, demands them back [?], and through this present humiliation he calls me to repay them and to amend." What, then, did the ungrateful maidservant [?] do? With what words of comfort did she come to her kind mistress? She ought to have considered the righteous woman's whole life. She ought to have given up her senseless attempt and helped her by joining her in prayer. She ought to have humbled herself with her at the time of petition, toiled with her in earnest supplication, and lifted her up with words of hope. She ought to have joined in pushing away the unfamiliar adornment brought out of season by others. She ought to have sent it back and protested that it was out of place and foreign to her mistress's dignity. But far from intending any of this, she went further with her words. She pressed harder and hurled taunts at the righteous woman that were harsher than those of the Jews. She tore open the wounds of childlessness and scraped them raw. She even declared that her fellow tribesmen had not been unjust in making her a figure of tragedy. What, then, did the most noble and high-minded Anne do? She did not turn on the reproaching girl with the anger she might reasonably have felt. She did not expose the girl's folly or hold it up to public shame. She did not push her away and throw her out for her ungrateful rebellion, nor subject her to just punishment as unworthy to serve in her household. Instead, overlooking everything with surpassing magnanimity, she slipped out of the house and went to the [?] quiet spot in the garden. There she was free of all commotion, and [?] of quiet [?] she reached the spot in the garden. Gregory of Nyssa, [?] narratives of Samuel: and having entered the Holy of Holies, she becomes a suppliant of God, asking not to fall short of the blessing the law promises, though she had in no way sinned against the law, but to become a mother and dedicate her child to God. [?] imitates [?], wrote [?]; of the garden, as one who had entered the Holy of Holies. When into the garden [?]…

And why did she not find some secluded inner room and raise her hidden and [?] prayer to God there? Because there her desire would not have been fully satisfied. She had many things in her mind that she meant to bring out in prayer, but she would not have been able to lay them bare before God with a clear mind, because of the commotion at home and the disturbances of fellow tribesmen who came to visit. For the same reason she did not go to the temple to offer her words of petition to the Master there, even though it had been set apart as a place of prayer for all her people. Even the temple could not give her the time of quiet she sought, for she had reason to expect many things that would interrupt it. She thought to herself that earlier, when she and her husband were already bringing offerings to God and doing good to the whole people, the Jews who brought offerings with them had reproached them and sent them away out of envy. What taunts, then, would they not invent against her if they saw her alone, at an unusual hour, persisting in prayer? Nothing would stop Jewish folly from condemning her, in that state, as mad or drunk. This is how they treated the blessed prophetess, her namesake, the earlier Anna, I mean Hannah. Those who seemed more reasonable than the rest, because they held the priesthood, attacked her harshly. They reproached her with drunkenness and slandered her converse with God. She sent up that fervent supplication from a [?] and sober mind, but they took her sobriety for drunkenness and her speech about God for babbling. Drunk with their own lawlessness, they mocked her. Yet the blessed woman did not cry out or bother those listening with disorderly sounds, for Eli the priest had already silenced her, and she spoke quietly. "And Eli the priest," Scripture says, "watched her mouth. She was speaking in her heart, and her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. And Eli's servant said to her, 'How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine, and go from the presence of the Lord.'" How, then, could Eli think she was drunk, if he saw her speaking with God in prayer? If from the first he had silenced her
[?] to her by a certain young servant [?], by one at the age most given to recklessness and to mocking what is good: "How long will you be drunk?" And therefore [?]…

with a rebuke, and if nothing came out of her mouth of the kind that comes from people in that state? For the words of the drunk and the rowdy are unseemly. Even when others force them to be quiet and beat them hard, they let out those shameless shouts, and their appearance is as disorderly as their words. But what unseemly thing did she do to give proof of drunkenness? What unseemly sounds did she make? What good order of sober people did she break? Was it that, when condemned to silence, she accepted the rebuke? Was it that the dignity of her outward bearing revealed the state of her mind? Was it that she kept silent the flame of prayer burning within her and showed its fervour only by the movement of her lips? "For she," Scripture says, "was speaking in her heart, and her lips moved, but her voice was not heard." Should they not have been amazed at her extraordinary endurance? Ought they not to have admired the steadiness of her bearing, her ceaseless and silent petition to God, her eyes lifted constantly toward heaven, and the unspoken, or rather soundless, groans that came from her anguished heart? For she did not let even these be heard. That is why it says, "Her voice was not heard." They shut her out from words and articulate speech, but she held back even sounds without words, so as to give the mockers no excuse. This is how she raised her petitions to God, with such wonderful endurance. And what does the servant who insolently mocked her say? [?] "How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine, and go from the presence of the Lord." What wine are you ordering her to put away? Her burning longing for God? Her sober mind? Her endurance in fasting? The prayers she sent up from a fervent soul? And where are you sending her, away from the presence of the Lord, when she has given up everything else and seeks his face alone? Her longing for him lives in her heart. She sees him as the only one who hears her words, and with the eyes of her mind she [?] him rather in the [?] of the tabernacle…

[?] So it was that at the time of prayer the mockers attacked the Anna of old. But the new Anne, the wisest of all, feared that she might suffer something like this while she offered her earnest petition. So she withdrew from the temple just as she had withdrawn from the house. She went to the more solitary spot in the garden because it was quiet, and she wisely foresaw that there the purity of the prayer she longed to offer would be kept safe. Or perhaps she did this not for that reason but because of the truth now made plain, and so already proclaimed by her actions what would come of her. Those appointed to serve the shadow of the customs of the Law confined to the temple not only the sacrifices offered as gifts but also prayers for their pressing needs. They believed that their requests were more likely to be granted there. Anne, whose name means "grace", shows in advance, through a petition and a spiritual offering brought to God

in this way, that grace was already beginning to be no longer confined to one place in people's minds. For the grace of God, who is in all things, is present in everything. It will work its own benefits in all things, in people's beliefs as it already does in fact. Righteous Joachim foretold this too. He withdrew from the temple and offered that acceptable and wonderful petition on the mountain. In this way he showed that when the new grace came, the temple would be left bereft of the shadows tied to one place, and the rays of grace's light would reach everything that exists. But what were the words of Anne's prayer in the garden? It is good to bring them into our discourse and to see how fitting they are. In other places, too, she offered her prayer, and even if it took different forms, it still kept a consistent order. But here it came rather from a broken and humbled soul, and it was heard as something new and extraordinary. The righteous woman began to offer her supplication in proper order, and in the manner of a lament she brought into her words that blessed humility. So she did not compare herself only with people of her own kind and race and say that she was unworthy and had been deprived of their blessing and grace. She declared that she was wholly cut off even from sharing the blessing given to the irrational animals and to lifeless creation. That is why, in the prayer she uttered alone, she mentioned birds and four-footed creatures, wild beasts and the earth and what grows in it, the waters and the creatures born in them. She did this to show how useless she was, and so to draw God, who alone is most compassionate, to mercy. But God anticipated her words. Before the petition she offered had come to an end, he announced to her that her requests would be granted beyond all hope. "For behold," Scripture says, "while she was speaking, an angel of the Lord came and said to her: 'God has heard your petition. You will conceive and give birth, and your offspring will be spoken of in the whole world.'" He heard her, for he knew the words of her petition before she had thought of them, and in a way beyond words he weighed them. He heard her petition, for it was he who moved her to make it and made it ready to be heard. He heard the prayer that came from a broken soul, for that is why he rests in such a soul and delights in its humility. He heard her petition, for he had proclaimed its fulfilment beforehand through the voices of the prophets. He heard her prayer, for he would make its fruit heard throughout creation. "For your offspring," it says, "will be spoken of in the whole world." Her much-celebrated glory will be spoken of throughout the world: her one renowned fruit, the famous ornament of all creatures. The eloquent mouth of human nature will be spoken of, the

[?] a defence for those who will keep silent. Glorious things will be spoken of her among every rational nature, and [?] powers will hymn her mighty deeds and proclaim her glory. "Your seed will be spoken of in all the world." "For you, O Anna," he says, "do not show such persistent endurance and wage the struggles of prayer so much for the sake of continuing your family line and the fruitfulness of nature (for you bear to God the fruit of an abundance of virtues), as because of the report about your childbearing that will be heard among your people. You want to be freed from the reproach of childlessness, to be counted and spoken of among mothers, and not to be shut out from their blessing. But the fruit of your prayer and the fertility of your nature will be spoken of and magnified not only in Israel or among your fellow tribesmen. It will be noised abroad through the whole world: among kings and rulers, among priests and the righteous, among nations of many tongues, among the wise and the unwise. Among so many will your fruit be spoken of. Resounding in the ears of so many, it will be magnified as its own wonders deserve." What, then, does the blessed and great-souled Anna do? What gift does she give in return to the one who grants her such a blessing? How does she repay her benefactor for his gifts? What whole burnt offerings of thanksgiving does she promise to bring? Not costly votive gifts, not sacrifices of irrational animals, not the firstfruits of crops, nor any other of the fine offerings that people bring in return. She offers the very fruitfulness of nature that had been given to her, the very offspring she had prayed and longed for. For its sake persistent prayers had been offered and abundant tears poured out [?]. For its sake she had shown strenuous endurance and disregarded everything that makes for comfort. "As the Lord my God lives," she says, "if I bear a child, whether male or female, I will bring it as a gift to the Lord my God, and it shall minister to him all its days." See Anna's burning longing for God! See her surpassing greatness of soul! See how, by this dedication, she also showed how freely she offered to God the fruit of external goods. For if she dedicates to God with such fervent resolve the blessing of nature given to her, the joy of her soul and the consolation of her toils, what of the rest of creation would she have spared? What of her more precious possessions would she not have consecrated to him? And consider the generosity of her mind. She does not specify, "If the child happens to be male, I will give it to the Lord God," but says, "whether it be male or female." What she promised was the vow of an insatiable love for God, the sign of an irrepressible longing for him. She says that he alone has the prior right, as to choose among all other things, so also to receive the fruit of nature, whatever it might be. For had she said, "If the child be male, I will bring it to the Lord God," and passed over the female in silence, she would have been thought to mutilate the whole dedication by what was left unsaid in her promise. But as it is, by including both male

and female in her vow, she showed her unspeakable love for the God she put first, and left her words free of any other suspicion. And yet nowhere in Scripture would one find a female dedicated to God in vows or consecrations, and least of all counted among those who minister in the temple. Nevertheless, in the excess of her love for God, she introduces this novelty into her vow, prophesying the novelty that was to come about in fact. For she alone of womankind, the sole firstfruits of humanity, was both promised and rendered to God as an offering honoured above all. O promise that cannot fail! O vow announcing in advance benefits beyond the reason of nature! O most holy offering! O God-loving resolve, which renders to God the fruit of its own hope in such a form and in such a manner! In what respect will this not surpass Abraham's whole burnt offering? In the long time of prayer that preceded her? In the moment of the prayer itself? In the manner of the oracle given from God? Or in the greatness of soul shown in the vow? Let us pass over in silence how far the offering itself transcends his, for it admits no comparison, since God alone is honoured above it among all creatures. But let the most fervent love for God of the one who offered it be admired and praised. For she too made an offering, as Abraham did. But he was fulfilling obedience to a command, while she was rendering the fruit of her own free choice. He brought an only son, born by reason of the promise rather than of natural childbearing; she brought the one and only blessing of her nature, which she had received as the fruit of many toils and intense prayer. For rewards of good things beyond all reason are the work of toils and of struggles beyond measure. Given wings by toils, prayers are borne up to God. By toils the great work of virtue is accomplished. By toils, as by fire, the soul comes to be proved. The enjoyment of eternal goods is the reward of toils. By toils the turning towards God, an ascent [?] [The following appears to be an intruded note:] This Joseph, being old and a widower, by the necessity of the lots cast among widowers and unmarried men from each tribe for the virgins of the temple, since firstborn children, both male and female, were dedicated in the temple, received the holy Virgin Mary by lot. There Joseph, since he was [?] ... this one in the temple, as she reached the first bloom of youth, her parents brought and dedicated. That it had come forth to me [?] ... ministering to him all the days.

and with it intimacy [with God] naturally comes about. As for the reward of toils, true reason judges that things beyond understanding are given in exchange, even for some cheap and small things. For what toil could anyone not only undertake but even conceive that might be thought to balance the smallest fraction of those goods? By the works of what struggles could one ascend to heaven? Ladders made of what toils could reach such a height? What sweat spent in this perishable and fleeting life is repaid with things eternal and blessed? What toils could anyone show worthy of intimacy with the Creator, by which he might make himself a fit dwelling for God to inhabit? For "I will dwell in them," he says, "and walk among them." And again: "I and the Father will come." This is the goal of the goods we hope for. This is the kingdom of heaven. This is the enjoyment of eternal delight. This is unending gladness, perpetual exultation, a reward that surpasses not only all toil but every mind. Do you see that no toil can be measured against the blessed enjoyment of the goods laid up for us, or even be thought of beside it? Yet though our struggles fall so far short, and the sweat we shed for virtue is so inferior to those rewards beyond reason, nevertheless the supremely good Master will give an enjoyment beyond conception in return for the cheapest and smallest toils. For compared with the blessedness there, the toils of human effort are reckoned small and of no account, even if a person wears out his whole life in them, even if he makes his whole life one continuous contest. Even if he multiplied his life a hundredfold, or twice that, or three times, or ten thousand times, and so extended the span of the years in which he carried out the persistent struggles of virtue, he would appear to have struggled for nothing in comparison with the rewards hoped for. Therefore, by small and cheap toils let us win the unsurpassable rewards; let us store up the wealth of inexhaustible goods. When I say small and cheap, I do not mean only the toils that seem so, but also the continual struggles of a whole life, the persistent contest of virtue, the toils spent unceasingly and fervently for its sake. For such are the rewards of the munificent Master, such is the overflowing wealth of his recompenses. In the excess of his love for humankind and his goodness he gives eternal goods in exchange for perishable ones, infinite goods for few, rich goods for poor. For he has no need of what is offered; he desires only the salvation of those who offer. Therefore the only rich Giver looks with favour not so much on the quantity of what is offered as on the quality of the offerers' intention. He has an incomprehensible sea of compas-

-sion. He is Goodness itself, the sole abundance of good things. He arranged the present delight for the sake of the gladness to come. Through the mighty works of his own mother he raises our lowliness up to himself. Through her extraordinary wonders he provides, beyond all hope, for human salvation. For this is the purpose of his whole economy. For these things we speak solemnly of your mysteries too, O Theotokos. For the refashioning brought about through them we offer you unceasing thanksgiving. For this, as we hold your other feasts, so we hold this notable festival for you. For this reason we proclaim together the achievements of the forefathers. Today we glorify the greatness of their virtue. We praise the fervour of their love for God, their surpassing endurance, the prayers that were heard, the oracles that foretold our salvation. And we honour you, the glorious fruit of them and of nature, the root of good things, the source of eternal gifts. For this reason we put you forward today as mediatrix with the one born of you, and them as intercessors with you. We ask through them, or rather through you (for you need no intermediaries, lover of the good), that the gladness we find in your great works be preserved for us without end. Through you we ask the one who beyond all reason took flesh from you to grant that the present delight may be followed by the blessedness of the world to come; that this choir on earth may be exchanged for eternal glorification; that in place of hymns that fall silent he may give the never-silent sound of those who keep festival, sent up to him with the voice of exultation and confession [?]. For he is gladness and exultation and unending delight, and to him belong honour, glory and worship, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen. Homily III.

Homily on the Conception and Birth of Our Most Holy Lady, the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary. Today the earth shines with a heaven in the flashing rays of grace. It is resplendent with a heaven in spiritual brilliance. It is adorned with a heaven above the world. For it receives, at her birth, the higher heaven, truly brighter than light and most spacious, a heaven that holds no setting sun but makes the never-setting Sun rise on the world, a heaven adorned not with visible stars but with spiritual torches. This is what we celebrate today. This has spread before us the most splendid banquet. This has gathered the present choir. This has roused our speech and calls everyone to share in it. Come, then! Heeding the call that has rung out for all to hear, let none of those invited miss this sweet delight that belongs to the whole world. Let no one be deprived of the common delight and

boast of our nature. Let us all share in the feast set before us. For it has been set before all alike, and prepared for the gladness of all and for a glory exalted above all glory. Human nature had indeed already received many great benefits from God. It had been honoured with various graces, through which the Benefactor conveyed glory to our common nature by means of those who shared in those graces [?]. But by none of them all has it been exalted so highly as by this present munificent and divine honour. Therefore, forgetting what went before and putting the old things behind it, it is lifted up and exalted together with this magnificent glory. For what among the gifts God had given it could be thought to bear comparison with what is present now? What is bringing our nature into being out of nothing, compared with putting it on when it had been corrupted and reshaping it again in a new formation? What is honouring it with being made in the image, compared with adopting it as a son? What is earthly rule and authority, compared with now reigning with the Master of all in heaven? What were the sights shown to those who saw God, in visions and dreams and in the appearance of the gentlest breeze, compared with the One who was seen in them being seen by us in his very being and dwelling among us in his love for humankind? What was the election of prophets and righteous men, and the glory that came to our race through them, compared with the boast of our nature being taken to be Mother of the God who chose them, and with this magnificent honour coming to us through her? This is our glory beyond all measure. This is what all must welcome and embrace today, rejoicing and honouring it with praises as far as they can. Some might say that such gladness and thanksgiving belong rather to the Lord's appearing, since all these things came about through it and it is the fulfilment of the mystery and of the gifts bestowed. But let those who argue this understand that today's delight was the cause of that one. It is the beginning of his reconciliation with us and of the gladness that dawned on us through that appearing. Pledges received at a reconciliation are symbols of a firm peace, and from them begins the delight that the reconciled enjoy through its blessings. A woman chosen from among the subjects and taken into the royal family becomes an unfailing token, for the people from whom she was chosen, of their union in kinship with the king and of the honour that will come to them from it. When a palace is founded on private land, it becomes an unmistakable sign to the neighbourhood that the one for whom it is being built will be present and reside there, and through it the neighbourhood already welcomes his kindly care and protection. In the same way the events of today have come about, and [have proclaimed beforehand] the approaches of the highest glory. [Note (12): "Superum gloria" (the glory of those above) [?] ... the approaches of the highest glory. The word ἐφόδους [?] ...]

proclaimed beforehand the approaches of the highest glory. The [?] ... she became a mother and did not become a bride. But he calls the betrothed a wife, just as Scripture is accustomed to call men bridegrooms even before [?]

the bride has been chosen, and the palace has been opened [another reading: brought forth] and made ready today. And the certainty of what was hoped for came to us, the sharers in the gifts, through the King's coming to dwell with us and his union with us. So today's brightness leads the way to the gladness of the ineffable economy. It leads the way not as though it were separate from that gladness or set apart from it in greatness, but as guiding us towards the security of the whole. And it does so fittingly [?] and first of all for us, since it was through one of our own that it brought about the most perfect joy. For this reason, as we offer this thanksgiving for the forefeast, which is also the cause of the final feast, we must crown the present festival with praises, bright in outward appearance but brighter still in the order of our souls. We must leap for joy more cheerfully, rejoice more spiritually than bodily, vie with the exultation of the spiritual and divine ranks, and all urge the whole creation to rise up in these things. But the choir of angels anticipates the speech that summons it, and today it praises the one through whom it saw the fulfilment of the mystery. The heavens also anticipate it, and honour the heights of the new and supreme firmament. The luminaries run ahead and are more brightly illumined by the rays of the spiritual Sun of the cloud. The earth comes of its own accord, glorying and exulting in its own offspring. The nature of the waters, leaping with new leaps, brings gifts [perhaps: forms an escort] to the one who procured its sanctification. Since all things today display their own boldness, I for my part would more fittingly summon our own nature, the closest of kin, crying aloud: Come to me, every age and every rank, all of the earthly order and all of the order above it; priests and kings, and you who display the heavenly state and citizenship among those below; rulers and ruled, old and young, virgins and mothers, barren women, and you who are infants in innocence. With a more divine gladness let us welcome this day of salvation and sing its praises. For on this day was born the boast that suits all alike. On this day, from barren loins, sprang the adornment of priests, royal power, the perfection of the virtuous, the ru-

-lers' and the ruled's untroubled good order, the understanding of infants, the beauty of virgins, the [gathering and] crown of mothers, the fruitfulness of the childless, the undoing of barrenness. From a barren woman blossomed the abundance of good things; from righteous parents the most righteous fruit grew. But who are these, and where did they come from? Let me be allowed to relate what concerns them, not so as to exalt it with praises worthy of it (for that, I think, is beyond not only our power but anyone's), but to show how they were preferred out of our nature, and how, having obtained an unsurpassable grace, they became the cause of God's munificence towards our race. For what conceptions, even of orators, could rise to the greatness of these matters, let alone contrive to treat them in proportion to their eminence? Panegyrists take as their material the deeds and the grace from God that came to the people they praise because of those deeds, and, so far as their rhetorical skill allows, they try to inflate what is before them so that it seems more wonderful, rather than winning for them a fitting glory. But when the achievements of the righteous are trumpeted by a munificence beyond conception, what display by encomiasts [would suffice?] [?]? What extraordinary honour could be found for the most extraordinary of all? For what could be conceived among all that has been from the beginning that could guide our praise by analogy? Consider, I beg you, the election and preference [?] of all the righteous, and their closeness to the God who chose them, and you will see the incomparable pre-eminence of Joachim and Anna. You will see their dignity, honoured and glorified beyond all conception. For the Creator chose them for the renewal of a world grown old. From them he takes the mother through whom he willed to provide for the new formation. From their blood, as being more royal in virtues, he puts on the royal purple of our race. [This shows that they stand above all the righteous.] This is the surpassing privilege given them: to be chosen alone out of all, to be brought into being at the due time, and to be taken up for the fulfilment of the mystery. Consider, then, how their story escapes every attempt at comparison. It is not words but the facts before us that trumpet this. But it would be profitable both for the festival and for making their excellences plain if we unfolded a few brief points from the history that narrates their story, for in this way it would show us more clearly the truth of what is said. To quote the account from the beginning [another reading: in its very words], it runs as follows: "In the histories of the twelve tribes of Israel," it says, "there was a certain Joachim, who was very rich." The opening of the writing was composed with intense praise, so as to show by a clearer sign the greatness of what follows. What does "in the histories" mean to indicate? "In the genealogies," it says, "of the twelve tribes of Israel."

From this, then, he shows that Joachim traced his descent from a royal line that had remained unmixed from of old. Honoured for the good order of his ancestors and for his own, he was a man of distinction and singled out, preferred among the tribes of Israel. Next the writer offers his wealth as a proof of his eminence, and at the same time he speaks of his righteousness, which was entirely his own and stood above that of all his fellow tribesmen. “For he offered,” it says, “double gifts to the Lord.” Truly he was rich with a double wealth. By consecrating double gifts he made sure that the treasures of this present, passing life grew smaller, while the treasures of the life that abides forever grew larger. Or is it not plain that he would not let even passing wealth remain with him, but cut himself back every day to what was enough? The text itself points to this: “For he offered his gifts to the Lord double, saying within himself: Let what is from my abundance be for all the people, and what is for my forgiveness be for the Lord my God.” See how far this goes beyond the righteousness of the law! Consider how the evangelical way of life of the apostles was achieved beforehand in these righteous people, or better, surpassed. “Let what is from my abundance be for all the people.” He means: let me keep nothing beyond what is necessary. Let whatever exceeds my need be set before all the people. Let what I have in abundance be [?] held in common. O most just mind and judgment, when wealth has been gathered into treasuries that no thief can break into! So their virtue stood above others from the very beginning. But next another achievement of theirs comes to light, and it goes further still. Having cut their wealth back to what was enough, they then brought to the God of all, out of what they had, everything the law prescribed for new moons, the customary offerings, the sacrifices for release from sin and the purifications of the body. “And what is for my forgiveness, for the Lord my God.” So they cut down their property not only to what was enough but even to the point of want. The words “saying within himself” are also [?] of special note. Along with the great wisdom of his good counsel, they show signs of the speaker's eminence. He did not do these things by looking to others or by paying attention to some example. He found the good by himself and carried it out himself. Old precepts and laws did not lead him by the hand to such an achievement. He himself began the doing of good works and became a lawgiver in practice for those who came after him. See how rightly these were preferred above all the righteous. I say rightly, not with regard to the gift of the mystery, for grace is beyond any reward for works, but by comparison with those who share their nature. But it is fitting to follow the sequence of the story.

It says that at one of the notable feasts, as he was bringing his gifts in the usual way, his fellow tribesmen heaped reproach on him because he had no children. “It is not lawful for you,” it says, “to offer your gifts, since you have raised up no offspring in Israel.” Some copies have: “It is not lawful for you to offer first.” It is likely, then, that because he was

righteous and dignified by a double nobility, he was given first place in the offering of gifts, as he was in everything. To the envious this was unbearable. They had nothing in his life to accuse. To them he was not only beyond reproach but plainly beyond rivalry in his excellence. So they threw his childlessness at him as a pretext, charging that he did not keep the law. Yet this came from the highest providence: that the righteous couple remained childless until then, and that they were then raised up to bear a child through prayer. The first showed their boldness before God, for when they asked, their request was not put off. The second worked together with the appointed time of the mystery that God had been pleased to bring about. So the righteous man, reproached as one rejected, was grieved beyond measure. He was not stung by the words or ashamed of the matter. He was afraid that he had overlooked some divine commandment, and that this had brought about his rejection by God and had come to light through men. [For thus, having already received the unerring oracle that showed his reconciliation through enigmatic signs, he did not seek childbearing.] So exacting an auditor was he, both in fulfilling the law and in examining the hidden things of his conscience; so fully did he regard everything that concerned him as a matter of divine providence. That is why he did not quarrel or answer their words. Nor did he plead that he had never before been barred from the customary rites because his life and his gifts were blameless. As soon as he received the rebuke of their reproach, he fled to God, the examiner of secret things, and took the wilderness as his ally in his converse with Him. He did not share his intention with his wife, though she showed herself of one mind with him, nor did he [?] entrust the care of outside affairs to his household. Who, even in our own day, has shown such unwavering hope in God and such contempt for present things? Still less in his time, when even the more modest and prescribed virtues were hard to fulfil. [?] “And on the next day,” it says, “he offered his gifts, and Joachim said: If the Lord is gracious to me, the plate of the priest will make it plain to me. And he looked at the priest's plate. He also went up to the altar of the Lord and saw no sin in himself. And Joachim said: Now I know that the Lord has [?] been greatly gracious to me and has forgiven all my sins. And I went down from the mountain [?]…”

Let us now set aside the story of the patriarch Abraham. Some might think he should be left out of the comparison, both because of his age, since he was one of the ancients, and because of how high his righteousness stood. Yet if anyone wished to compare these too, he would see how far superior our present subjects are. To Abraham both his migration and the land where he would sojourn were announced. What is more, the One who cannot lie promised him in advance an end to childlessness and to the barrenness of [?] his wife. Holding him by a promise, God fed his hope and encouraged him in his petition. What could be seen as more heartening than a promise from God? Joachim had no promise. He believed that all things impossible are accomplished by the One who is able, and that nature is reshaped. He rested his hope on God's unseen providence, and so he both separated himself from his household and kept up an unceasing converse with God in prayer. Abraham asks for a sign that he will possess the land and that his race will increase [and demands to know how the promises will be fulfilled]. Joachim, however, was as undoubting when his prayer was heard and an angel brought the good news of the birth as he had been while he prayed. He does not ask how the announcement will come true, nor does he seek signs to show that his weak nature will be healed. He held the message to be as good as fulfilled, and even after he was assured of the birth [variant: after the assurance], the only signs he looked for were signs that he was seen as pure by God alone. The marvel of the sacrifice also invites examination here, but it must be passed over. Abraham sacrificed at God's command, while Joachim offered his sacrifice of his own free choice. Joachim's child was an only child in the proper sense, while Abraham's was so by reason of the promise. Abraham brought his son and then received a victim to offer in his place, while Joachim truly consecrated his child, offered her as a whole burnt offering, gave her up and brought her as an offering. Abraham offered a patriarch of tribes and a righteous man; Joachim offered the Mother of God, the most righteous Lady of the patriarchs. This undertaking goes beyond not only the present comparison but every comparison. You see how far this righteous man's merits outstripped his. Now look also at his stay in the wilderness and his endurance beyond nature. It would be right to call it an angelic way of life, for it stands strange and unmatched when deeds and words are compared. The story says he continued in prayer forty days and nights without food, nourished only by his hope in God. “For he fasted forty days and nights, saying: I will not go down [another reading: go up] either for food or for drink.” Some of our more ascetic strivers have judged this astonishing, and others even impossible. For this achievement is beyond human strength, since only the Creator

of nature sustains its endurance by the choice of His will. The righteous man made Him his [?] unfailing support and forcibly rose above the needs of the body. From Him he received the grace to succeed in struggles beyond his strength and to obtain gifts beyond his hopes. Moses, it is true, is admired for fasting the same number of days, and what he did is certainly not without wonder. But if anyone wishes to search out and examine the endurance of each, he will find a difference here too, in the way the thing was done. Moses was sustained by the limit set by the One who gave the command, by the keeping of the tablets and by his very waiting on the Lawgiver. With this greater strength he lightened both the long stretch of time and the needs of nature. Joachim [?] was not cheered by anything else. Strengthened only by a hope that could not deceive, he took on the solitude and the struggles and put forward his intense prayer. Who would not marvel at this and count it beyond all words, since its greatness of soul overcomes all reasoning? If anyone suspects the present words of exaggerating these virtues, let him set the facts out bare and examine them himself. For it is hardly possible even to keep up with their praises, even if the one attempting it were among the most celebrated, let alone to raise them above all. Such, then, is the story of Joachim. The story of his wife Anna, who shared his ways, is great and marvellous. Far from falling short of her partner in grace, it goes further. For she [?] completed the struggles of endurance alone. Her husband had gone away to sojourn who knew where, and she had to bear the taunts about her childlessness, which were [?] worse than this. Contending against these, she prevailed with hope and faith as her allies. Twofold, too, was the reproach she suffered: first from her fellow tribesmen, then from her maidservant, and this last, when it was brought, made the rebuke most painful. Reproaches from strangers do not usually wound their target as much as those from people closer to home, especially when they come from those placed under one's authority. How, then, does this most noble woman respond? None of these things wounds her invincible hope. She shakes off the adornment improperly offered to her, removes her mourning garment and puts on the pure bridal one together with the divine robe. So she prepares for prayer with adornment of both kinds, so that pure [?]… “The day of the Lord has drawn near” … [?] to have put on a mourning robe. [?]

…she sends up to the God of all. But she found a quiet and undisturbed spot in the garden, and there, as in a hidden inner room, she secretly offered her prayer in her grief. Since she was practising a prayer of the heart, one that needed more time, she did not bring it out into the open before those who reproached her. They would have condemned her for drunkenness, as they did the earlier Hannah, or for babbling. If they had recently attacked her with mockery when she sought God's favour at the proper time, what more stinging words would they not have let fly at so unaccustomed a persistence? That is why neither she nor the great-souled Joachim hurried to the temple to offer their prayers. They rightly thought their prayer would be welcome and no burden if it were made at greater leisure and in quiet. But the more fitting and surer reason is this. They were forerunners and heralds of grace both in deed and in name, for Joachim is interpreted “laid up” and Anna “grace”. So through themselves they were weaving in this way the boundless breadth of grace: they withdrew from the temple, but they sought the favour of the Maker of all in every place. So much for this account. Their prayer is presented as worth noting for both of them. It recounts all the mighty works of God, both the things He brought into being from nothing and the things He made new in wondrous ways by reshaping the natures of things. In this way the benefits granted to the righteous are set forth: thus Abraham and Sarah, thus the story of Hannah and Samuel are brought forward by righteous people. Giving thanks for like favours, they ask for equal grace, and with more and more earnest persistence they seek not to miss what corresponds to them. After this, the prayer of blessed Anna in the garden was very different, and it gained a ready hearing through the contrition of her soul. She did not use words and ideas of petition. With lofty humility she lamented and confessed her own lowliness. She placed herself below all creation and went through each kind of thing that shares in the Creator's blessing. The Creator's compassionate care is inclined to nod in favour of such conduct and such words, more than of words spoken about one's own particular case. So she says: “I, [?] wretched woman, am more useless than all created things. Everything serves your command, Master, but I alone am utterly deprived of such blessing and grace, unworthy of the good fortune of my race. For this too is fruitful for you, and its very existence shows how different I am. I am a stranger to the fertility of the many kinds of living things, for they too have received a like blessing. The earth bears abundantly, ceaselessly bringing forth plenty at your command. Meadows bear fruit, and the lovely shoots of plants

bear fruit, putting forth fruit in season and most sweet, and through the thanksgiving of those who share in it they send up glory to you. I have no share in their grace, since I judge myself unworthy to be counted among these, which are the works of your goodness.” What excess of humility do these words not display? What contrite heart has the soul that puts forward such thoughts not shown? How would the Lover of good not accept such a disposition above every fragrance and offering? How would He not nod in favour of such a prayer, above a whole burnt sacrifice, He who delights so greatly in such wholeness? For “a sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.” Such are the merits of the righteous and the stories told of them. These bright marks of their virtues flashed out the noble beauty of their souls, more radiant than anything visible. It was fitting that the gift without equal among those born should come forth from a surpassing election. It was fitting that the all-holy wealth should gush forth from abundant virtues. It was fitting that such fruit should be gathered from such labours: that the noblest shoot should sprout from a noble root, and the best branch should spring from good loins. She is the ever-blooming ornament of the race, the loveliest shoot of nature, the lofty stem of the mystery. From her the flower of immortality sprang up and breathed out an everlasting fragrance, and its fruit becomes life, incorruption and permanence for all who share in it. Offered up with such labours and words, the prayer of the righteous couple came to its fulfilment through a divine message to each of them. Angels appeared and announced that the prayer had been heard and that the birth beyond hope would come to pass. Angels bring the good news of the conception of her who is more honourable than the angels. Angels announce in advance the end of barrenness and foretell that through it the dividing wall of sin will be broken down. Angels herald the conception beyond hope of her who brought about a conception supernatural and ineffable. Angels run ahead of the birth pangs of her through whom the pains of our first mother came to an end; her coming forth was beyond expectation and her birth a marvel. From a husbandry without hope, the helplessness of barrenness foreshadows, in a fruitfulness beyond thought, the renewal of nature. To the child born, the circumstances of her own birth provide proof of the newest mystery. In what happened to her, the strange childbirth is confirmed in advance. In the wonder worked for her parents, the more ineffable wonder is taught.
