For this one heralds that one, and through the things that were fulfilled it proclaimed in advance the certainty of what was proclaimed. Here a barren woman, shut out from what is natural; there a Virgin, walled about by inviolable purity. Here a bond of long standing; there the undefiled manner, immortal [?]. Here the birth is the fruit of good deeds and prayer; there

through incomparable virtue and surpassing purity a conception beyond telling is newly brought about. Here an angel heralds deliverance from birth pangs; there an archangel brings the good news of the supernatural conception. The promise in the present good tidings proclaimed what concerned her even more clearly in advance. “Your offspring will be spoken of by all,” says the one who foretold it to Anna. It will be spoken of and proclaimed not only on earth but also in heaven. What is to be said about it will resound not only in human ears but also in divine minds. See how David foretold these things. He proclaimed the outcome of future events as though it had already happened, signifying the inescapable truth of what was to come by using the past tense: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God.” Glorious beyond every glory that can be told. Glorified by the highest powers; honoured and longed for by humans, who share her nature; desired by the patriarchs; revered by the forefathers; written down and sought after by the prophets. Because of this all creation rejoices. In this the angelic hosts rejoice together. With this the whole world is adorned. In this the nature of the earthborn exults today. Glorifying these things, it keeps the festival that goes before the greatest salvation, and it embraces in advance the one through whom it has gained the most perfect joy. For this birth announced humanity's rebirth in advance. It proclaimed beforehand our recall from error and our refashioning from what had grown old. It foretold that our barrenness and fruitlessness in ignorance would grow into fruitfulness in the knowledge of God. It paved our way into grace. It opened the gates of salvation in advance. It has been set forth for reconciliation. It has been taken up for mediation. Because of it we now share boldly in God's race. Because of it we have received a closer standing with God. Because of the bridal chamber that has been born, we have been counted in the royal wedding hall. Because of the heaven, brighter and wider, now brought forth, we have enrolled ourselves in the heavenly way of life. Through the blessing of our kinswoman we enjoy the delight of the Gospel. But you, who bring about our present and future gladness, you who are the pride of our boldness and our honour: repay the banquet held for your festivals with the banquet on high. Adorn the one who is zealous for these things with great gifts [?] in return. Order the present assembly with spiritual as well as visible brightness. Let a harmonious song sound in this divinely gathered choir, a song of the joy of those who keep festival in heaven. Look upon the mind of each. Examine the ardour of our longing and show it to the Master, who examines the unspoken things of the conscience. Present our disposition to Him who openly sees what is hidden. He has indeed seen it,

for He knows all things unseen, and He perceives the longing for you that the hymn singers feel for His sake. But in His great goodness He wills that these things be both presented and fulfilled through a mother's intercession. This is your glory before Him, and ours before you. It is also the token of His love for humankind that came about through you. Raised up together with the hopes this brings, we despise our own lowliness and forget our earthbound, earthy way of life. Hence we are eager to rise from the earth and hasten toward heaven. Hence come our unfailing hopes of the good things stored up for us. Hence our expectation of eternal things. Therefore, as we keep this notable and divine feast with warm hearts, we send up [another reading: offer] our thanksgiving to Him who arranged all things for His own glory, for His mother's boast and for [?] our saving adornment: to Christ, the cause and giver of all good things. To Him belong honour, worship and glory, with [?] the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

By George, monk and chartophylax of the Great Church: Encomium on the Presentation of the All-Holy Theotokos in the Temple and Her Dedication to God, According to the Story. Bright is the sign of the present feast, and so it urges the assembly gathered for it toward boundless light. Splendid is the evidence of the present words, and it promises that the themes will bear fruit full of glory. For see, the festival of the Virgin has shone upon us and directed our minds spiritually toward itself. Like a settled spring it has cleared the sky for our speech, and it has turned the winter of silence into the calm of speaking. Come, then, guided by her rays, let us eagerly and intently direct the course of our speech toward her. [Variant titles:] “By George the Chartophylax, who later became metropolitan [?]”; and in the Sforza manuscript, with [?]: “By George, monk”

…and let each of us crown her with such praise as lies within his power. For even if all of us fall short of what she deserves, let us at least try to excel in eagerness and to outdo one another in the intensity of our resolve. What speech could touch even the smallest part of her worth? What speech could boast of coming near it even in bare imagination, let alone try to grasp it in full? The praises of the Virgin have flown beyond every power of speech, and so they have set their bounds beyond all praise. For my part, my friends, before I was caught by the passion of longing, I judged harshly the boldness of those who attempted this. It seemed madness to me to lay hands on what is beyond one's power, on things whose accounts lie beyond all speech. But since I have been overpowered by the one who leads me and drawn into the venture of the many, I now stand with them as a suppliant asking for pardon, having learned by experience of this passion how inexcusable the attempt is. So if any of you tries to charge me with presumption, let him judge what lies before us to be not the arrogance of rashness but an abundance of longing. Its overwhelming force has driven us to dare the greatest things, with faith leading the way and hope lifting us up together toward them. For words of praise are offered not for the glory of those who are praised but for the piety of those who speak. That is why the attempt seems to me quite free of danger. The Divine, too, being by nature in need of nothing, and being itself glory and the majesty of those it praises, offers itself as the cause and occasion of praise to all who wish to praise it. It receives no increase of its own glory, but it welcomes the eagerness of those who offer praise. Since this is how matters stand, come, let us take up the words of the present feast and apply our zeal to the things we have been moved to speak about. But what skill of rhetoric could handle the present subject methodically, so as to work out a fitting sequence for each point in its order? What comparison could be set beside it to show a likeness to one whose equal has not been seen since the beginning of time? Those who unfold subjects of this kind set equal beside like, or greater beside lesser, as far as the matter allows, and in this way they hunt down an abundance of words. That is why it is very easy for them to examine what they have found, and their judgment of what is said turns out true. But where the bounds of nature have been overcome, there the rules of encomium are too weak to serve. So let no one try to subject what is exempt from nature to the same rules as what follows nature. The one has no fitting common ground with the other, since each shows how far apart they stand. Hence the loftiness of the subject seems to me hard to grasp, and it does not seem possible to set out the main points that arise from it by the rules of comparison. Still, even if the present subject is wholly exempt from the ordinary course of things, it is possible for us not to run away from our longing, lest by failing in our desire we be robbed of piety along with it.

The serpent's venom entered us from the beginning, smouldered within us, and consumed the race. Spreading constantly through each individual, it was no longer checked in its spread, and no protective remedy could be found to wipe it away. Like a festering wound it worked its way into everyone alike and ravaged each new generation. The Creator therefore wished to remove it, to show his own power and to heal the wounded. So he contrived to raise up the fallen against the one who had wounded him, and to put victory into his hands, and in this way he made public a splendid trophy and the defeat of the destroyer. This could happen in no other way than for the physician to put on the nature of the sick man and, under a gentle form, draw the destroyer to himself, so that the destroyer, running up as to something familiar, would fall upon the unexpected. In this way the disease would more easily be stopped, its cause being reduced to utter powerlessness. Since this was how things were ordered, the cure had to spring up from the same root from which the evil had first set out, and the evil had to be driven out by the same road by which it had entered the race. That road was the pliancy of woman, which had unwarily opened the entrance and spread the ruin to herself, to her husband, and to those who came after. And this is exactly what he brings about. But now that I have come close to the subject, the impossibility of the task restrains my speech, and my mind is struck dumb by the greatness of the wonder, as I see a strange and astonishing mystery being accomplished on earth, and the salvation that was ineffably promised before the ages now reaching its fulfilment. This, clearly, is the praise that belongs to those who begot the Virgin; this is a prelude that escapes every advance of speech. The mind that applies itself to it, though it has not failed, is carried out of itself. Let anyone who examines these things consider how great a wonder has appeared from this. Out of sheer love for mankind we were brought by our Maker from non-being into being. We were commanded to dwell in paradise for the sake of good works. We thoughtlessly thrust the commandment away, and by our own choice we drew death upon ourselves. Freedom was promised by the Creator; but the deed was delayed, and time kept searching for those fit for it. Generations passed by. Prophecies were laid down one after another. The patriarchs and all the righteous lived in hope. Abraham passed away, and so did those after him, who had been initiated in symbols into the mysteries of that day and gazed eagerly toward the outcome of what was to come. The divine Moses, who clearly beheld the types of the mystery and understood the truth, seemed to think that what had been foreshown would be fulfilled in his own time. In the wilderness there was hope. Among the judges who led the people there was expectation. Samuel received oracles. David proclaimed that the day was near, and then he departed. The choir of the prophets loudly proclaimed it and announced that Christ was

at the door. All of them ran their course without obtaining what they hoped for, since the time, and with it those who were worthy, had not yet come. At last it found its own, sprung from the same stock and made ready by the Creator for this purpose. I mean Joachim and Anna, who gave birth to the one through whom what had been foretold would be fulfilled. They put into action the first steps of the prophecies. They put forth the root of what had been awaited. They laid the foundation of what had been promised. From them was fashioned for us the vessel of the healing ointment. From them rose the one who brings us gladness. From them came the pledges that prepared the way for joy. Because of their surpassing virtue they became known to the Creator beyond all others, and indeed they had been foreknown and appointed to serve divine mysteries. That is why, having walked every path of the commandment, they reached the summit of perfection, and they alone obtained what very many had longed for since the beginning of time. For although they shared in our common nature, they carried off an exceptional glory. Those through whom the greatest things are accomplished receive a greater glory than those for whose sake they are brought to completion, and all the more so, the more closely the accomplishment belongs to them. And here one could not even suspect that anything comes closer than those who were taken up to serve as mediators of these wondrous works. For the Word built his tabernacle for himself from their very clay, and from her, in a way beyond understanding, he took human clay, arranging both deed and thought in a wholly new way. Such, then, was the way they carried out every good work, and yet they were marked out by childlessness; and through the affliction of trial the hidden excellences of their virtue were made public. For the customary precepts of the law judged piety by fruitfulness in children and reckoned flourishing offspring an unfailing proof of blessing, and on that basis they decided what was acceptable among the sacrifices of atonement. Not unreasonably, I think, and not prescribing anything out of keeping with the dullness of the people they were leading. For people then were inclined to the bodily, hiding the goods of the soul beneath the increase of the flesh; and being strangers to the abundant gifts of the Spirit, they judged from these things what was acceptable to God. Those who served the shadow and kept this custom therefore refused the gifts the righteous couple offered because they had no children. They did not think it lawful to disturb, in their case, the fixed order of the laws, which had been kept until then. But some will probably try to raise a difficulty for us here. They will say: “If the parents of the all-pure one had been chosen for this, how is it that the gift of children was shut off from them until then, and they spent most of their lives childless? Especially since the mystery

was foreordained to take its beginning in them, and it had been proclaimed that she who was to serve it would come forth from them? If they fulfilled without fault all that the law then required; if they had stored up an abundant swarm of virtues and carried even more abundantly the things by which people of that time judged perfection, how did they fail to obtain the very means by which they were to reach the goal? How was it that through the affliction of childlessness they checked the course of the prophecies? And how was it that the beginnings did not appear in abundance from those from whom the Word was hastening to take up our common nature?” Yet the following will be seen as a true defense. When the steward of things to come and Creator of all wishes to carry out one of his hidden designs, he does not lay the foundation of what is to come through the increase and abundance of nature. Instead he prepares the future through the abundance of his power and through the helplessness of circumstances. This is what is most proper to God, while what follows the course of nature is not the most wonderful. So when he promised Abraham that his descendants would be like the stars in number and like the sand of the sea, he did not bring this about through any good fortune of nature. He fulfilled the promise through signs of weakness and by his own power. In this way he brought forth Samuel. In this way he sent John as herald of the divine plan. And anyone who examines most of the things that have come to us in wondrous ways will see that they came about not according to what seems fitting to most people, but according to what befits [?] the Cause

For my part, I do not stop the solution at this point; another explanation, not implausible, comes to mind. What is it? Otherwise their piety would not have been made plain to the people of that time, and their closeness to God, confirmed through prayer, would not have repelled the contentious talk of the doubters. But as it was, having come to need this, they showed at once what intimacy with God they had in other matters as well, since what could be seen made public what was hidden in them. So when the righteous couple moved to prayer, they hoped for an answer that was not in doubt. They did not reason this way: “If the one who knows hidden things had known that our having children would turn out well, he would not have shut up our nature or condemned our life to barrenness.” Instead they urged each other to look to Abraham and Sarah and Hannah, and they encouraged each other to receive, as those had, the fulfilment of their prayer. “These,” one says, “are set before us as a fine example, if we offer our prayer without doubting. A fine proof is Sarah's barrenness, changed into the tenderness of youth. A fine sign is she who was bent with age and was refashioned to the vigor of limbs in their prime. Let us look to Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, who through prayer laid aside the same affliction as ours. Let us learn from her perseverance in petition and the fire of her mind. Let us recognize how she too,

reproached as we are, did not give up praying. Let us imitate her. Let us hasten to follow in her footsteps. She leads us by the hand to ask for what we hope for, and through what she accomplished she promises us success.” The righteous couple put this counsel into practice, and so from then on they chanted the words of this prayer: “Lord, you promised the patriarch to multiply his descendants beyond the number of the sand of the sea. You did not do this through many children; you fulfilled the promise through the offspring of one. You gave possession of the land as an inheritance not to many, but to this one. You changed Sarah's barrenness into childbearing. You strengthened her feeble limbs to serve your command. You turned her unbelief into faith and changed her doubting into a mind free of doubt. We do not laugh, as she did; we make supplication, as Hannah did. We do not doubt in our prayer; we believe in its fulfilment. You worked wonders for our fathers. You blessed Jacob and renamed him Israel, hinting by this at his power to see God. You arranged the journey of his descendants into Egypt and their preservation there. You did not allow the murderous Egyptians to diminish your people. You punished them with unbearable plagues for their disobedience, so that your love for mankind might be shown and their cruelty made plain. You opened a strange new road in the sea. You made the elements act in a new way. You turned the flowing nature of water into a solid form and led your people across on a dry path. You rained down abundant food in the wilderness and fed your hungry people until they were full. You made water gush from the jagged rock and gave your thirsty people drink. Looking to these things, we do not hold back our prayer through doubt; we stretch out our hope in sincerity. Lord, you have brought into being out of nothing the things that were brought forth. Will you not, then, lend your help, O lover of mankind, to what lies within our power according to your original decree? If you blended into fellowship things wholly different in kind, will you not restore to their proper state things united by nature that have grown weak? If you brought nature into being when it did not exist, will you not, as Lord, set it right when it is in a poor state? This, Master, is your work. Yours is the achievement that is impossible for all others. By your might the greatest wonders are worked. At your command the currents of rivers run backward. At your bidding the sun halts in its course. At your nod the many kinds of dumb creatures remain fruitful and continue from generation to generation. Everything yields to your ordinance, and nothing resists your command. You changed Hannah, who suffered the same childlessness, into a mother of many children, and you made the woman with many children childless. We too bear reproach, Master. It does not come from one fellow wife; it is loudly bewailed by our whole

tribe. You are able to take it away. You are able to make the idleness of nature ready to bear fruit. So we have set our mind on you alone, and we will turn nowhere else until we see what we ask for fulfilled. For we know that he who in other matters has been quick to anticipate our requests will not delay.” Such was the prayer of the righteous couple. It proved the sincerity of their faith, and by what they said it revealed their good standing in other matters as well. It was a first sketch of their hidden piety. For the words that come forth reveal the disposition from which they came. The words that are brought forth become symbols of the things hidden within that are not otherwise shown. The mind brings forth the word, and the word announces the affections of the soul. It makes the hidden plain and lays the foundations of what is done. So the prayer of the righteous couple was brought to fulfilment, and therefore the future was revealed to them by a divine oracle. O wondrous success! O prayer that pierced the heavens and flew up to the very throne of glory! O words that hymned a greatness beyond words! When the mother received what had been announced as though it were already present, she promised to consecrate to God the child she would bear and to dedicate it in the temple. What is this, Anna (so I might say to her)? Why do you run ahead of what is still to come? Why does your eagerness get ahead of what is being announced? Why do you promise to bring to God what has not yet come to be, as though you already held it in your hands? You ought to have waited for the time of labor and then dedicated the gift that came from you to the one who gave it. You ought to have taken into account the uncertain outcome, so as not to fail in your promises by announcing them in advance. O the faith of the righteous! O mark of a great-souled mother! She did not weigh the future with doubt. She did not put off what had been announced out of hesitation. She did not consider her own nature, unfit for this until then. She did not take up an argument against it because of how hard and unusual it was. She did not wrap her soul in anguish over what seemed impossible. She was not at a loss, reasoning with herself as others usually do: “Might the oracle turn out to be a deception? Might my long barrenness stand in the way of the promise? Might the one who appeared have come bringing good news only to comfort me? Look, I am past my youth. Look, the bloom of my prime is withering with time. Look, the strength of my limbs is hurrying toward weakness. Most of my life has run its course. The time that lets parents delight in their children is slipping away. The joy of having children holds its sweetness at the start and hopes to reap its fruits in old age. Why do I busy myself with prayer and promise?” Anna let no such thought enter her reasoning. As soon as she had offered her prayer and been told by the one who appeared that it would be granted, she hurried with burning eagerness to bring the child to the temple, as though she already held what she was waiting for. What speech could praise the fervor of her faith,

through which she did not fail to obtain what she asked, and through which her mind was not wounded by the stings of doubt? What she achieved was truly the work of unwavering faith, the faith by which all the prophets were convinced of things to come as though they were present. The divine Paul defines it truly when he says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.” What is hoped for seems to belong to things that do not exist: it does not subsist in itself and cannot be seen at the time it is needed. Its outcome is uncertain because it is hidden, and it leans rather toward the unknown. So Paul shows that unwavering faith has the character of substance, because it gives real being to the existence of things hoped for and actively establishes itself in those who hope. And “the proof of things not seen” is what was once awaited in faith and, as time went on, was brought to fulfilment, setting forth the true outcome of things as a kind of proof. In the same way, the mystery of the Word, which is beyond understanding, was proclaimed long ago and awaited in faith, and when it was made manifest many ages later, faith showed the fulfilment of the thing as its proof. The righteous couple took hold of this faith and did not fail to obtain what they had asked and hoped for. So they gave birth to the spotless one, who brings about our rebirth and is the cause of our re-creation. Through her, what had been made in the image of God and had become worthless returned to its own beauty. Through her we cast off the tunics of sin and put on the robe of light. She is the cry of the prophets, the fulfilment of the divine oracles, the crown of our salvation. O how blessed were the parents in their child! O the birth that brought those who bore her goods beyond understanding! Among ourselves, when fathers happen to have children who are proclaimed for worldly distinction, or shine with the light of virtue, or show some noble and great feat of courage, no small glory comes to them from this, since by their share in a common nature they share in their children's renown. But in the case of these two, what surpassing glory could be imagined in which they did not win first place? But why should I weary my hearers by speaking at length? Just as the child they bore has received the highest glory, second only to the Creator, so they too have been allotted a glory beyond comparison with all other parents. When the divine child had been born, Anna called her friends together, saying: “Come, rejoice with me at my child's birth. Come, be glad at my labor. Come, see the woman who is nursing beyond all hope. Come, behold the rod that has sprung up from barren loins, and look upon the barren woman who has conceived. Come, learn the fruit of our reproaches, and tell the story of what our prayer accomplished. Run together eagerly and prepare the way for her coming to the temple. Adorn the [?]

[?] Light up the entrances. Make the processions bright with torches. Strike up [?]; sing wedding songs, and lead the child forward as a pure bride [?]. Fulfil with me the promises [made] to the Master. Clap your hands with me in thanksgiving, because the Lord has taken away the reproach from my house, because what we hoped for has not come to nothing. See, our prayers have been fulfilled in deed. See, the promise has reached its end. See, the child who was born I now dedicate in the house of God, as I promised. Come, [?], and let us together offer her to the Master as an acceptable gift.” So the mother, with eager intensity, pressed to fulfil her promise. But her daughter’s infancy held her back and forced a delay. It did not allow the parents to be deprived of her at once, but urged them to wait for a suitable age. For this reason they brought her to the temple when she was three years old: a truly precious offering, a dedication revered by angels, the supreme and most pure treasure. In her the treasures of grace were stored up. In her the wealth of the divine plan was ineffably laid away. In her the pledges of our salvation were kept in store. She was the undefiled vessel, the place that received the light [?], from which rays of salvation shone over the world. For it was fitting that the spotless one should choose the number three for herself, since through her the power of the Trinity was made manifest to those in the world. In her the covenant of the Father’s good pleasure was transacted. In her the Word came to dwell and put on our clay. In her the Spirit made its dwelling, [?] the undivided [?] of the Trinity. Through her the world, divided in three, was joined together in the one worship of God. Through her the one who divided it perished with a crash. Today the living temple is brought to the temple, she who is higher than the heavens and more spacious than all creation. Today she takes up her dwelling in the temple who by her childbearing brought the exiled human race back to its own hearth. Today the spiritual tabernacle announces the good news of grace to the order of the Law, and bids the letter give way to the spirit. Today the spotless ewe-lamb is offered to the temple like a sacrificial victim, she from whom the Lamb of God came forth and took away the sin of the world. Today the blameless dove, flying about in the inner sanctuaries of the temple, escapes the fowler of wickedness, rising higher than his snares. Today the receptacle of the [?], laid up in the temple, is made ready to receive the Word. For it was not fitting that the most pure dwelling should live among the [?] of the world. It was fitting that she be [?] to the blameless place, to receive there the beginnings of joy [?], to be allotted the pledge of blessing, the symbol of the mystery, [?]

Discourse of George, Metropolitan of Nicomedia, on the Entrance of the All-Holy Theotokos. The present festival shows us fine starting points for our themes. It has prepared fine paths of approach and laid fine foundations for our ascent, and it now draws our discourse up toward itself. Having raised the discourse on high, it lifts it [Sirmond: raises it] by grace to the heights of praise, and step by step it carries the praise from glory to glory. But the discourse cannot rise as high as the realities themselves. That is not possible. Having barely risen a little from the earthly depths, it is lifted only faintly toward the height of its subject. Come then, let us toil together with it. Let us lay aside the burden of the body, rise on the wing of the mind together with the festival, and eagerly follow the all-pure one as she hastens to go within the sanctuary. Let us gather ourselves in from our wandering outside and step onto the next forecourts of the discourse. For the beauty of meadows does not make the way in so desirable to those who wander about outside as the fragrant paradise of the Virgin’s praises makes her entrance attractive [Mai and Sirmond: makes the entrance] to those who seek it. This meadow, the most fragrant and most varied of meadows, also procures incorruption for those who gather its flowers [Mai and Sirmond: crowns those who gather]. For it does not [?] with spring flowers, whose seasonal delight soon withers. Instead it sends out the fragrance of grace and perfumes the senses, and with the sweetest of scents it charms the mind toward itself. For in the case of those [flowers], once the sense has taken its fill,

it does not take the same pleasure in those that appear later. In the case of these, however, the fragrance of the earlier ones lingers, while a greater longing arises for those still to come. There, the beauty of the sight withers along with time. Here, the loveliness brings the soul a delight that lasts forever. People who manage to set foot in the forecourt of a palace guess at the arrangement inside from what they see outside. What they have not perceived with the senses they infer with the mind, and they are lifted up by it. The same is shown to happen at the porches of praise. I think this holds in every case, but it will be found to hold not least in this one. For the opening words have been lifted to a height, and from them a splendid adornment of the subject appears, with many advances distinguished by glory and beauty. Our task, then, is to lift our eyes a little toward the entrance and to look, as far as we can, on the beauty that lies hidden. For it is impossible to tell out all its brightness [Mai and Sirmond: even if it is impossible to tell out all]. Come then, shall we advance in our discourse further inward, holding the queen herself as our guide going before us? But now I see the festival flashing with boundless light. My mind is illumined, I feel moved to leap for joy, and I picture the great things now being accomplished. I perceive angels dancing together, and everything strange and worthy of the order and beauty of the heavens. From this it seems to me that the grace of the one we are praising comes among us herself and fills everything. She fills the assembly with gladness and bestows her gifts without stint. So let us look to the hope of these things and all go in together, each paying what he owes. The speaker owes his words. The listener owes an attentive hearing. The one who serves owes the fulfilment of his task. And all whose duty it is to meet some need are urged toward the entrance. Let the words now lead the way, gathering what follows to themselves. The Virgin’s parents were already bringing her to the doors of the temple. Angels escorted her round about, and all the powers above the world rejoiced together. Even though they did not know the ineffable manner of the mystery, they ministered to her procession as servants [at the Master’s command?]. First they perceived her, seeing as intellectual beings do, that she was a precious vessel of virtues. She bore tokens of unblemished purity and kept her body [free?] from any mixture of passions. Then, not disobeying the command, they carried out their service. Then lamps of light brightened the entrance, and everything contained in the temple turned to festivity. Even the lifeless things, I think, rejoiced with the angels. So it falls to me too to join their dance, to burst out in a loud voice as though I had been present then, and to cry out to the temple: “She is entering now!” And it will fittingly be [?]: “Widen your courts,” I say, “to receive

her who has been shown broader than visible [Sirmond: than the visible] and invisible creation. In her the Uncontainable became contained, and he will squeeze the broad way of wickedness into the narrowest. Kindle a lamp of light and brighten the entrances. Raise a torch on high as a signal, and turn the world toward yourself, so that it may see the luminous cloud, come to share in her rays, and behold the fountain of light gushing from her. Throw open your gates and bring in the spiritual gate. The Word of God alone passed through it and kept it sealed, as he knows how. For though she has received the name of gate, she kept the condition of a virgin. She fulfilled the function of a gate, but did not break the seals of incorruption. Draw back the veil, so that the living veil of the Word may come within. She hid the Godhead within herself, and her material substance was not burned up by its fire. Receive the lampstand gilded by the Spirit, whose lamp lights up the ends of the earth. Through her the seven gifts of the Spirit were kindled and gave light to the surrounding world. Receive the life-bearing table on which the bread of our life was set out, feasting those who partake on ambrosia [Mai: filled those who partook with ambrosia]. From her the bowls of wisdom pour out the clear and most pure drink of knowledge. Adorn the Holy of Holies and receive the more-than-holy tabernacle that can contain the divine essence. She raised up our fallen dwelling and set up again the tent of our forefather that had been torn down [?]. Through her our members, broken apart by the transgression, were joined back into their own wholeness. Receive the all-golden censer, in which the Word kindled the flesh and filled the world with fragrance. In her the charges of disobedience were burned away. Through her the air is freed from the stench of defilements. Through her the [?] of the Spirit breathed upon humankind. Bring in the ark of sanctification, which held the Lawgiver himself within, [which carried the heavenly manna, which saved our nature from the flood of sin — from Mai and Sirmond], and which by her childbearing freed the world from all destruction. She is the treasure of the new covenant; [?] the glorious tablets inscribed by God, on which the Word [of the Father?] was written beyond reason and changed the coarseness of the letter of the Law into the lightness of the Spirit. Take the priestly rod, which blossomed out of faith with the unfading flower, the Lord. [Receive] the holy and desirable land, from which truth and righteousness sprang up, in which feet wrapped in decaying coverings are forbidden to walk. I mean [?] doubt [?]

[?] the shaded mountain, on which the Word was pleased to dwell. In her our nature, [overshadowed?], escaped the burning heat of sin. From her the cornerstone was cut out [?], crushed the image of the enemy, and winnowed it into dust. Receive the fruitful olive tree, from which the gladdening oil gushed out and anointed creation. [Receive] the glorious throne, the royal chariot on which the Word rode when he came to dwell among us in the flesh. [Receive] holy Zion, which the Creator chose and, in the plan of his providence, prepared before the ages. In her he was born according to the flesh, and coming forth from her he crushed the powers of the ungodly. Embrace Solomon’s couch, round which the sixty mighty men stand guard. These are the unerring prophecies of the divinely inspired Scripture. By what they foretold they bear witness to the validity of her divine motherhood. On her the Word lay down, rose up with flesh, and mightily struck down the tyrannical power of the enemy. The prophetic tongs prefigured her, which carried the coal and cleansed the lips, which were held by a seraph and are proclaimed by the Holy Spirit. The sealed book foretold her, which no one learned in letters could read except the one who sealed it and kept it sealed beyond reason. The most pure scroll revealed her, on which the Word was inscribed without writing and tore up the bond of deceit. She is [?] the queen who stands at God’s right hand, near [?] and in splendour. She is beautiful by nature and admits no blemish. She comes up from the Lebanon of virginity and perfumes the world. From her flows the sweetness that sweetened the ancient bitterness of the tree. Over her, lips were sweetened beyond honey, and the tongue welled up with gladness. The fragrance of her garments was sweeter than all the spices of the earth. Bring her in [?] as a bride, whose beauty is beyond compare and whose glory is beyond words. The light of her eyes surpassed [Sirmond: dried up] the rays of the sun. She is the enclosed garden that the thoughts of sin cannot enter. In her the divine plant sprang up without cultivation. It dried up, root and all, the first curse of the tree, which had run riot in life, and in its place it blossomed with blessing. She is truly the sealed fountain, from which the most pure streams [flow?] and water the world. In her the river of graces comes forth and circles the whole world under the sun. Receive the [light?] cloud, on which the one who rides on heavenly clouds threw down the idols of the Egyptians [Sirmond: of heavenly clouds, the]. Bring in the living city of God, which rejoices forever in the [streams?] of his [river?]. [Bring in] the sanctified tabernacle, the glorious house, the indestructible temple, of which you yourself stand as type and symbol. You now hold her as the true manifestation of [?]; her [?]

and as you bring her within, give way to her as the greater. Put an end, at this point, to symbols [and cease from riddles. How long will you cling to the shadow? — from Mai and Sirmond]. How long will you pride yourself on the letter? See, the rays of grace have shone out. See, the letter has passed over into the spirit. You have grown weary serving the types. See, the one who makes all things new is coming. So pass over from the law that has grown old to the ever-young grace of the Word. Why do you persist in dreams when you are receiving the one who brings about their fulfilment? Why are you sprinkled with the blood of sacrifices and wrapped in the smoke of burnt fat, when the one who commanded these things does not accept them? For the Word says to the Father: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me.” He is coming who will put an end to these with his own blood, and who cleanses our nature not of fleshly defilements but of sin. Redemption is at the doors. The proclamation is at your gates. Escort her [Sirmond: he sent her ahead], who runs ahead of the mystery to you. She carries within herself the fulfilment of the words revealed to you. Isaiah foretold her when he said: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.” Ezekiel called her the gate of God. David called her the ark of sanctification. [Jeremiah foretold her as the way — from Sirmond.] The bush on the mountain, burning yet not consumed, prefigured her to Moses. Receive her with joy. Run to her eagerly. Venerate her as higher than all creation, visible and invisible. Embrace this most pure dwelling. Bring in the spotless tabernacle, and drive out the bloodthirsty company of the Jews. Their murders of the prophets [Sirmond: proclamations] cry out loudly against them, and the blood cries out piercingly. Why are you defiled with the gore of their pollutions? Why are you stained with their lawlessness? Why do you cover up the profanity of their arrogance [and kindle the wrath of the Creator more fiercely? — from Mai and Sirmond]? Halt at this point the anger of the avenger. Do not inflame further the wrath of the one who formed you. For the more sins pile up, the greater the requital of punishment becomes. Indeed, it is heavier than the crimes committed, since it brings punishment that never dies. She bids you cease. She has come to take your place. She has received your glory in greater measure, for the end of all things has fallen to her lot. You displayed the types, and she has shown their fulfilment. As much as a shadow falls short of the body, a riddle of the truth, a word of the deed, and an image of the prototype that caused it, so much do you fall short of her brightness. For you receive reverence from one nation only, your own. She receives from all creation the most exalted

[?] having, not long after, [?] by the indwelling of the Word. Having received her, it will remain indestructible forever and will never be stripped of her glory. Depart from here, then, and give way to what is greater. Even if you wished to remain, that will not be left to you, since your own ministers have become the cause of your departure [?]. These things I have said to the temple [?] not unreasonably. They draw their credibility from what is seen now, and I think those who hear them accept them without needing proof, judging by the facts instead of by tests. Once the place broader than the heavens had been brought inside the temple, the customs [of the temple?] at once found in her a symbol of their own dissolution. They saw glory running of its own accord to her, while they themselves were being stripped bare day by day. Then Zacharias, who was serving as priest, was inspired with the gift of prophecy and rejoiced at the Virgin’s coming. He contemplated the unimaginable beauty of her soul, hidden in a woman’s form. He perceived that the undefiled one bore marks foreign to nature, even though she was clothed like everyone else. For her character was beyond compare, and her way of life was ordered by the virtues. Therefore, as she grew older year by year, the gifts of the Spirit grew greater in her. She conversed with angels and was not without divine visions. While she was spending time at the sanctuary as usual, Zacharias saw someone of strange appearance [?] hastening to go within the sanctuary [?]. It was fitting that she should be nurtured not in the Holy of Holies of the tabernacle but in heaven itself, she who had been shown to be broader than these [?] dedicated to the temple of God [?]

speaking with her and giving her food. The one who appeared was an angel. So Zacharias was amazed in his mind and reasoned to himself [Sirmond: concluded] like this: “What is this sight? It is truly strange and foreign to the customs of this place. The figure that appears is an angel’s, and it is talking with a young girl. A bodiless form brings what seems to be food for bodies [Mai: food fit for bodies]. An immaterial being gives a woman something material that can be seen. Visits from angels here are accustomed to come to the priests alone, to urge them toward what must be done or turn them from it, and even these do not appear often. But for what I now see to come to a woman is altogether unusual, and to one who is under age and still so young. If the girl before me were a married woman, shut off from the gift of childbearing by the affliction of barrenness and seeking offspring through prayer, and if that were why she was staying here, then what I see would be explained by her purpose. That did happen once, to Hannah and her household, but it is not always shown in our day. Now, however, the Virgin’s coming here has nothing to do with such things, and the [visits] of the one who appears are continual. For this reason wonder and fear both fall on me all the more, and doubts lurk around what is hidden [Mai: what is being hidden]. What then can this be? What has the angel come to announce? What is the food he brings? From what storehouses was it taken? Who prepared it? Whose hand baked this bread? It is not for angels to prepare what suits the needs of the body. Even though a great many have been fed through them, others prepared the right food beforehand, and the bodiless ones served their fellow servants by means of a body. The angel who ministered to Daniel had enough power from the one who commanded him to carry out the order himself rather than through another. But he took Habakkuk [Sirmond: of Habakkuk the] as an intermediary, so that the strangeness of the manner, the overwhelming sight, and the angels’ unfamiliarity with preparing food would not terrify the one being fed. And the raven that served Elijah did not learn the place [Sirmond: the where] by itself but was taught it by an angel. And what it carried came, I think, not from elsewhere but [?]

[?] comes to pass. And the matter belongs to things ineffable that do not fall within the reach of reasoning: the girl has received such gifts that bodiless beings submit to serving her. What is this great abundance of gifts? What has the Virgin done to deserve such things? That she surpassed in purity all the generations that have been, I know, convinced by the facts: her character is clear proof, and finally, having received the work [?]. But what could be the reason for her obtaining such great blessings? Perhaps the Virgin will be shown to bring us great benefits, by which she draws the Divine to herself. Will not the oracles of the prophets be fulfilled in her? Will not the end of what we hope for come to pass in her? Will not the One who is to come to restore our race take what is ours from her? For this mystery has been proclaimed beforehand, and the prophecy calls for such a one to serve it. Truly, then, no other has been foretold [or: chosen beforehand] for his service except the girl we see here. For I perceive in her the hidden and inconceivable beauty of purity, and God's kindness towards her reveals what is hidden. How blessed is the house of Israel, from which such a shoot has sprung! How blessed is the root of Jesse, from which this flourishing rod has grown up, which is to bear salvation as its flower for the world! How glorious beyond glory is the memory of those who bore you, beyond all blessedness! How glorified am I, who have delighted in such sights and who lead such a Virgin as a bride! I will be grateful to you forever, temple of the Lord, because by serving you I have not missed what all the righteous longed for. Today I have been magnified above all priests; today I have been glorified above all prophets. For what they were initiated into in shadows, I behold in its true beginnings. Such, it is likely, were the thoughts of Zacharias as he contemplated the Virgin's wonders, strange as they were and overcoming nature. And indeed they truly were so. O wondrous beginnings! O extraordinary signs! O growth of a body that received an increase of grace surpassing it! O that pure and radiant soul, which in a body still growing showed advantages beyond nature; which was not prevented by the body's immaturity from perfection in virtue; whose union with God was not broken off by her youth! Who has seen, who has heard of such growth in a body that lived in the holy place, was escorted by angels, and received ambrosial food? For souls, even when joined to the body, even if they should reach the summit of freedom from passion, would scarcely enjoy the food of angels,

if indeed Scripture hints that the food of angels is the unerring Word. But here bodily hands receive the pure food, and through them the spotless soul is filled with gifts. O surpassing purity! O growth in stature, what a ladder of holiness it set up to the heights of heaven: by it the Word came down to us in a strange descent; by it the earthly tent of our nature, which lay below, ran up to the heavens. But when you hear of the Virgin's strange way of life in the temple, do not doubt it; do not scrutinize with reasoning what is beyond thought; do not subject the incomparable to comparison. You see the strange new thing done in nature, and you doubt these things? You see the very Word of God ineffably dwelling in her womb, and you dispute about food that was immaterial and of another kind? You see the overshadowing of the Spirit in her by the Father's will, and you question the ministry of angels? Nothing about the all-pure one is doubtful; nothing about her greatness is unfitting. All things hold firm in truth. For the divine tabernacle had to grow by such ascents; the spotless ewe-lamb had to be feasted at such a banquet and filled with such foods. She had to be raised in her earliest years not in the Holy of Holies of the tabernacle but in the very heaven of heaven, she who was shown to be wider than the heavens and surpassed them in purity. She had to be served not by one angel only but escorted on every side by ten thousand times ten thousand. For him whom they cannot see, she [?] contained in her womb. Him who wraps himself in light as in a garment she wrapped in her own bosom. Him who holds all things in his palm, once made man, she held in her arms. Who, considering these things, would not think great things of his own nature? Who would not be lifted up in mind to the heights because of them, and consider himself above all things? [Who would not be heard speaking loftily because of them, and crying aloud to all creation?] Who would not become lofty-minded because of them, and be carried beyond his own lowliness [?]? For indeed beyond [?]

[?] ascent. We had fallen through the transgression; we had become unworthy of our Maker's care, finding nothing to excuse our being deceived. Our nature lay fallen; it needed someone to raise it up; and it found him, not through another but through its Creator himself. And the raising up was a strange one: not by command, as in the creation of old, but by a dispensation in keeping with his love for humankind. He did not entrust the work of raising us to angels, but kept for himself the works of condescension; and not only did he raise us up, he also took our nature on himself, and seated what he had assumed on the Father's throne. What shall I think in the face of this unspeakable love for humankind? With what words shall I praise this boundless condescension? With what praises shall I acclaim the Virgin through whom these things were brought about, through whom the recalling of the body came to pass? What honor could be shown equal to her purity? The Creator loved her and built his own tabernacle from her; he did not refuse to dwell in her; in her the Father's will was fulfilled; in her the all-holy Spirit came to rest. What glory will be found worthy of her, whose glory the Creator made higher than all except his own? O gift more honored than all honor! O loveliest adornment of all that is lovely! O Theotokos, supreme ornament of all that is good! By your childbearing beyond reason you raised up our ancient nobility from its fall; you restored to its own beauty the comeliness of the first image, which had been darkened; by your conceiving you turned the pangs in sorrow of our first mother into offspring of joy. Through you our exiled race has hastened back to its own dwelling; through you we have regained the pure delight of paradise; through you the turning sword has withdrawn; through you the closed gates of delight have opened the way in; through you the hopes of the prophets have come to fulfillment; in you their sayings have reached their end; through you we hold the unfailing tokens of our resurrection; through you we hope to attain the kingdom of heaven. We have you as the helper of our salvation; we have you as the champion who aids us; we put you forward as the mouth that speaks in our defense; we carry you about as the boast of our confidence. We, the multitude of Christians, have you as our strongest wall; faithful kings hold you as a mighty weapon; through you they crush the boldness of their enemies. You, Theotokos, do not overlook the prayer of those who ask continually; stretch out your hand to the weary; take hold of those tossed by the waves; still into [?]

calm the waves of wars; [turn] into a gentle breeze the winds of those who assail us; grant, since you are able, a fulfillment that answers our prayer. As Mother [towards the Son] you have a boldness that cannot be refused; you have invincible power; you have might that none can withstand. Let not the multitude of our sins overcome your measureless compassion; let not our wrongful deeds cut off your inconceivable mercy. For however great the multitude of our sins of ignorance may be, it is easily dissolved if only you will it. Nothing stands against your might; nothing fights against your power; all things yield to your bidding; all things give way to your command; all things serve your authority. Higher than the heavens and all created things, he who was born of you [?] … of the word lead by the hand [?]

[?] showing [?], would not be judged unreasonable to offer. I, for my part, thinking I had already brought my discourse to an end in what went before, put forward my excuse, since perplexity was besieging my longing and not allowing me, as the saying goes, to set my foot beyond the threshold, nor to attempt anything further beyond my strength. But this longing, set ablaze by a flame smoldering unseen within, and now fanned into a great blaze, could not hold back its rush in silence, and brought it out as it pressed to escape. Seeing, then, that the subject stretches on without end, and that the kindling is enough for a conflagration, let each of you present grant me, overpowered as I am by this passion, the sympathy of pardon. Or rather, why need I ask this of everyone, when many share its joy, and countless others do not hold the force of the matter against me [?]? And if the present discourse shows anything that serves the festival, let thanks go to what drove me on, which deserves praise, and which by its own victory has made the vanquished a crowned victor. But if it falls far short of what the festival deserves (and it will certainly fall short), let the [blame?] be laid on that longing, and let our excuses be judged reasonable. So let these things stand thus; and let us hold to what follows, asking the cause of our subject to be our guide.

Now while Zacharias was astonished at the paradox of the sight and, by a more divine inspiration, was conjecturing what was to come, what were the angels who watched over the temple likely to think of it? With what perplexities, intelligent beings though they were, did they try to resolve what they saw? For this was ineffable, revealed only to those to whom the One who reveals alone wished it revealed. It is likely that one of them raised such questions about it: “What is this strange sight? What is this escort? Who is she who is feasted by angels? What we see is paradoxical, and unknown even to us. A woman is seen who is beyond our understanding; in her alone the advantages of our nature have grown weak. Since she serves God's ineffable purposes, her end has been hidden from us. All the extraordinary ministries here are carried out through us at their proper times, for we are not ignorant of the causes of the petitions offered up: some we serve through [?] types, others we know through [?] studies. The converse of those who make petition to the Divine is always hidden neither from our nature nor even from human nature. But now the things concerning her, having escaped human nature, escape ours as well. For neither did she make petition beforehand for the beginnings of what is to come [?], nor did anyone on her behalf make known, by the customary intercession, what will be. And the one who serves her is united with us in what is common, but set apart from what is performed individually among us. His visits are unusual, and his converse with the girl wholly strange. What is

this great care for the Virgin? What is the hidden wonder in her? Angels surround her; she sends up praise in harmony with our choir; while still in the body she has surpassed our purity; she is a woman in visible form, yet the mystery perceived in her is beyond our nature. In her all things rejoice together; our ranks exult with her; this divine temple has received her and rises up to serve her. O vessel plainly full of grace! O earthly nature that has risen above its own characteristics! O measures incomparably surpassed by her! O what firstfruits of its own harvest human nature has brought to the Creator! What a gift it has dedicated! What an offering it has consecrated! Truly worthy of God, more mystical than our sacred mysteries, holier and purer than our purity. For our blamelessness, compared with her, falls wholly short of likeness to her, and cannot rise to her holiness and spotlessness, which are beyond reason. And yet even if this were judged equal to ours, it would appear exceedingly marvelous, having strangeness in its novelty. For this is no great thing for us, who are free from matter and removed from its defilements. For those whose nature is unsuited to what is worse, the wonder of unchangeableness is not strange. So in one yoked to matter and yet vying with our spotlessness, this would appear paradoxical and beyond all astonishment. How could it not be judged so, when she has acquired beyond nature what is foreign to her nature, and, forcibly soaring up from what is her own, succeeds in rising to our advantages? In this Virgin, then, I flee [?] even from the paradox of likeness; she is marveled at as surpassing it. For what escapes our comprehension plainly does not refuse to be among the things above us. In what way is this hidden thing veiled? By what benefits is it [?]? By what dispensations is it kept? Of old, when God was doing good to the human race, the grace of his care was not laid down unseen. For when things received the beginning of their outcome, knowledge of their end came from that to those who searched rightly. But where the manner is overshadowed, knowledge has escaped entirely.”

Such things, I think, the angels stationed in the temple were thinking and puzzling over, while rejoicing at the strangeness of what they saw. And not only were they so disposed; among the people present too a single shared gladness had already arisen, for they received the Virgin as a cause of joy. And indeed we perceive that the history shows this, setting out her story in this way. For it says, “Every house of Israel loved

Mary.” Well done, the word [?]: how fittingly it suits the matter, how surely it made the future clear! What then does the saying hint at? It means that nothing remained without a share in the great joy over her; nothing that exists was left without part in the common exultation; all things were greeting their own salvation in advance. Not that the mysteries of the Virgin were being honored [?], but the things to come were being prefigured; or rather, already possessing through her, in potential, what was to be, they came to this joy at the benefit. For how could they not be wounded by this new sight? How could they not be enchanted by the beauty they saw: one young in body yet soaring above the things of the body; a child who had escaped the habits of her age; a virgin exempt from the defilements of nature; an offshoot of our race, companion of the angels; the form of weakness, risen above the marks of manly strength; within the holy places, dancing about as their own adornment; dwelling in the inner sanctuary, the revelation of the ineffable. And see how unerring the prophecy is; see how exact and infallible, how by the meaning of its words it made the matter plain. For it did not refer to the people alone, but by the name “Israel” it foretold the love that would attach to her from those who would come to know her. For nearly whenever divine Scripture wishes to signify the Hebrew tribe, it calls it simply “people,” as in “Rejoice, you nations, with his people,” and “My people,” it says, “has not understood.” But whenever it wishes to point to both that people and the people who truly recognize him, it indicates this by the name “Israel.” The name itself plainly confirms this, since every mind of those who see God is and is called Israel. Since, then, the Jews, covered by unbelief as by darkness and willfully refusing to look at the rays of truth, were to be blinded by God, the word passed over the name that properly designates them and indicated the shared affection of those who were to come. And if we see that “the people of the Lord” and “He saves his people” signify the greatest closeness to the Creator, so in truth it was, and the greater share belonged to that people. But since it willingly tore itself away from that closeness, senselessly leapt away from salvation, and wandered far from the One who called it, the word indicated those who would be made his own through the mind's vision, as they would be. And it did not say, “The whole house of Israel,” but, “Every house of Israel,” by dropping the article confirming the addition of those who would come after. Since things stood thus, nothing of this kind was hidden from the priest. So, being taught what was to come by the

Spirit, he paid great reverence to her who was full of grace. For he could not help regarding what was to come about through her as a greater cause of salvation. First, he considered her character and beauty, which were beyond virtue. Then he observed the ministry of the angel, which announced something great to her, and which did not stop at what was seen but hinted at something else, more wondrous still. For the angel's frequent visits to her foreshadowed the coming of Gabriel: God was both announcing it beforehand and accustoming the Virgin to it. The food brought to her was an image of the very bread of life, its likeness easily recognized by those with discernment, even though it differs in the greatest respect. For just as the manner in which that food was prepared, and how God supplied it, is unknown, so too the reason for the Word's incarnation and the cause of the mystery are hidden. The undefiled Virgin, partaking of that food, was enriched with divine graces; and those who come to share in this bread are filled with the gifts of the Spirit. But that food did not bring about cleansing from sins, for she who partook of it was not subject to them, being pure and in need of no [cleansing]; whereas here, along with the bestowal of graces, comes also the removal of sins. How, then, could Zacharias, struck by these things, not be filled with admiration? What surpassing honor would he not have paid to Mary, full of grace? What would he not have wished to think or do in order to devote to her all that is glorious [?]? For what of hers did not prove to surpass human things? Which of her smallest traits did not exceed the advantages of the great? For even what seems lesser in her is recognized as greater than what among us is beyond compare. See how, while not yet out of infancy, she was a stranger to its ways. For when she was brought to the temple and parted from her parents, she suffered none of the violence of nature's tyranny; nor did separation from her parents loosen that unchanging resolve of her soul; nor, gazing after them with untroubled eye, was she stirred within in her thoughts, though she was still almost clinging to her mother's breast and [suckling]. This is truly worthy of wonder, [?] that sinless mind [?], and especially when the bond is one of parental ties, in which fears do not dismay, pleasures do not beguile, but affection remains unharmed and is not cut off by bodily separation. An infant torn by force from its mother's arms cries out against the injustice by its very posture and voice, stretching out its hands to the one who bore it, and piteously and

…full of tears, its eye continually [?], sending out a mournful voice with weeping and calling for the mother who bore it, the child makes its suffering known to all. No threat or fear silences it, and the finest precious things, if someone gives them, do not soften it. It holds fast to what it wants and turns to none of the things offered, knowing only one remedy for the griefs that grip it: to cling once more to its mother's bosom. But she, pure of every human habit and passion, unconquered by these things and higher than the constraint of nature, by none of them [?] a mind untouched by pleasure [?]. And although the separation had lasted a long time, she was not grieved even by this. What mind, however pure, has reached in its full maturity such freedom from passion as this all-spotless one showed in her infancy? What soul, what reasoning, what intellect has in old age [?] chosen the good and cast off the worse as she did in her youth [?]? For toward the very highest of these…

For my part, I am astonished not for this reason alone, but also because the purity of the all-blameless Mary, while still in the bloom of the body, surpasses the nature of immaterial beings. With advancing age this would not be judged so great, hidden as it is in the mystery. And why should we marvel only at her not turning back toward her own family, when we see that her parents too were made great in this? For they did not resent being separated from their dearest one, their parental hearts were not stirred, and they were not wounded by the goad of nature so as to turn back to the child and embrace her with their accustomed longing. No sweet, lisping words of hers came to mind and troubled their thoughts. No picture of her face, her company and her beauty, painted in the mind as things once enjoyed, grieved them more sharply. For a good that is gained does not bring as much joy as a good that is taken away brings grief. What has never been experienced is possessed only in desire; but for one who has come to enjoy it, its loss brings sharper pain. And above all, when the things we care about most are absent, despondency comes upon us in abundance. It would have been natural, then, if the righteous couple had been distressed at this, for one of them to say to the other: “What has the persistence of our many prayers gained us? What lasting gift of God has it left us? What profit is there in the pains of labor? What consolation for [?]? The gifts of childbearing are enjoyed not in the birth pangs but in the years of growing up. In due time comes comfort for one's labors, the fulfillment of one's expectation, and the hope that the child will inherit the blessing of those who bore it.

But what such comfort is left to us, whose toil has no end and whose hope lies in darkness?” Such words the righteous would naturally have spoken, if they had felt anything merely human. But they rose above all this, and holding her who had been dedicated to God as though she were in their hands, they not only cast away words of despondency but sincerely offered words of thanksgiving, as those who had themselves produced such fruit, who had consecrated their own firstfruits to God, who had set the newly blossomed shoot within the holy place. O most acceptable sacrifice of the righteous! O offering dedicated as a ransom for the world! O good root that put forth the best of shoots! With what words shall I praise Joachim and Anna? With what flowers of praise shall I adorn their crown? With what thoughts shall I reach for their wonder, which is beyond thought? But what can a variety of words add for those whose glory and crown is the joy that came forth from them; whose exultation and ornament is the common gladness of our race; who are clothed with a precious adornment, the Virgin who is higher than all honor, the bright and glorious diadem, the radiant and many-lighted splendor, the [?] brighter than every brilliance? She is their praise beyond this world; she is their [?] glory; she is their wealth that cannot be taken away, pouring out its abundance for endless ages. O their good fortune! O virtue that gathered such fruits! Great indeed it is, and beyond all fruitfulness. Since they were such as the discourse has shown, why need we ask whether they grieved ignobly in their souls at being parted from their child?

Now while she was spending her time in the temple like an angel, the time arrived at which women are required to keep away from the holy things. The Jews would not keep silent about it [?], and the people urged that she, as one woman among all others, be barred from the sanctuary, quite unreasonably and without inquiry. For they did not yet know the wonder of holiness hidden in her. For I think, judging by the truth, that none of the natural impurities was ever found in her all-spotless body, but that everything in her was made new in a strange way, just like the conception that was to come. Zacharias, understanding this, did not of his own accord consider sending the Virgin away, thinking it better to offend against custom and the people than to lose good things by her departure. But as the people pressed him on this, he fell into perplexity, thinking and saying such things as these: “What shall I do about this? What course shall I choose in the present necessity? With what aim in view can I avoid provoking God by rashness? Shall I lead the Virgin out of the temple? But the strangeness of the ineffable sights frightens me, and the wonder of the maiden astounds me; I fear that by wronging her I may pay the penalty for my presumption. For no one but me has delighted in her mys-

teries, and sin is counted more against those who know than against those who do not. Shall I keep her in the sanctuary? [?] The Jewish crowd is in uproar and puts forward lawlessness to support its own opinion. It does not understand how the matter stands; it does not know the mystery of the divine plan; it has not recognized the Virgin's purity, which is beyond nature; it knows nothing of her all-spotless mind; and for that reason it hurries her departure from here. I ought to face danger for her, since I have been initiated into the matter; I ought to be put to death rather than hand her over carelessly and rouse God against myself. But I fear that even if that happened, unworthy hands would be armed against her, would touch her all-blameless body and drive her out of the temple by force; that profane mouths would let loose insulting words against her and revile that inviolable one [?]. And who among men would receive her? Who is fit to bring her into his own dwelling? What house could receive without being straitened her for whom even this most wondrous temple is not a fitting [?] shelter; whose perfect purity it reveres; whose greatness it marvels at; whose wonders astound it? What hands could serve her whom angels served, whom they fed where she had dwelt [?]? Who would have the strength to look upon the beauty of such a one [?], in which the eye of God delights, in whose purity he exults, by whose loveliness he is adorned? What food will appear worthy of her whom the Word of God has filled, whom grace has filled, and [?] the storehouse of the needy? Who among all would be found worthy of these things, so that God's sacred trust might not be outraged by the unworthy?”

Such were the thoughts of Zacharias, as one who had learned the Virgin's mysteries more clearly. And one who thought this way about them was bound to be at a loss. If, then, he came to such amazement and wonder while still being initiated into the beginning of the mystery, how shall we not be astonished, who possess its end, and how shall we not, with joy and longing, extol her through whom it was accomplished? How shall we not proclaim her great deeds with a loud voice? How shall we not praise her in words, even though every power of praise is too weak to grasp these things? And why need I say this about praise, when the mind and understanding themselves are defeated by them? For speech is even poorer in resources here. What the mind often discovers, speech has no strength to express; and one can see the wonder of the Virgin exalted within, but diminished outwardly by the lack of means. Since I myself experience this [?], I accept the statement without witnesses, supplying its proof from my own experience. But since these things have been acknowledged thus, let us leave the examination of them to her, as one who knows all things, and let us ask her to measure our gratitude not by our words but by our thoughts. But, O Theotokos, most longed-for name, do not overlook the brevity

of what has been said, since it comes from a greater desire but a lesser power; receive it and do not reject it. Grant abundance to what is still to be said, and do not turn away our petitions. By your intercessions halt the wars against your people; with your mighty power defend the flock that trusts in you. We hold up no stronger trophy than your help. One thing only do we hope for that is mightier than it: the power of your Son. Or rather, for this too we owe the grace to you; for since we are always offending him, we remain neglected, unworthy of his care. But you, by your mediation, reconcile us, since in imitation of him you love what is good. You bend his boundless compassion to pity us; you keep up a sleepless intercession for us. For this is worthy both of his love for humanity and of your protection. This is why he took you as the firstfruits of our race. So that he might order our affairs through you, he made himself a debtor to human nature. We owe the punishment for transgression; he in turn owed the saving plan of his love for humanity. For these two greatest things we ask his grace: for the flesh he took from you, and for you, the firstfruits offered to him from among us. The request is reasonable, the expectation good, the hope unfailing. For although the swarm of our sins opposes us, makes war, and shuts out the benefits of his love for humanity, there is still no multitude of failings that could overcome his goodness. We know how prone our nature is to slip; we know how utterly unworthy it is; we are not ignorant of how countless our failings are; and for this reason we put you forward as our mediator. Do you see how all the hope of the people that bears your Son's name hangs upon you? Grant then, by your power, that it may end in good. This people has no other refuge from the terrors that beset it except your unconquerable alliance. On you its rulers have fastened their expectations. You they hold up in place of all weapons. You they wear as shield and breastplate; you they carry as a crown of boasting; you they have made the stronghold of their kingdom; to you they have entrusted the scepters of power. Arise, then, in great might before the face of the people and scatter the enemies of your Son, so that, freed from their godless madness, we may celebrate together in gladness and exultation, and, magnifying your all-glorious and most longed-for name, may worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; for to the Trinity belong glory, might, honor and worship, to the ages of ages. Amen.

Homily on the text: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother and his mother's sister”; and on the burial of the divine body of our Lord Jesus Christ, on Holy and Great Friday.

Our discourse has run up to a very high lookout, and with a sound louder than a trumpet it calls all creation to itself. For having gone up with the one who went up to the height of the cross, it has forgotten its own lowliness, and lifted up together with the sublimity of these events, it sends out a bright cry that can be heard far and wide. For what could appear to us loftier or more radiant than the present mystery, through which we have been snatched out of the lowest and darkest depths of Hades and brought to dwell in a heavenly and ever-luminous home; through which we have put off the gloomy covering of sin and clothed ourselves in the shining robe of adoption as sons? For through condemnation freedom came to us; through sufferings, freedom from suffering. Through death we, who were held in the iron prisons of Death, were carried over to eternal life. So these events are radiant for us and of the highest majesty, but fearful and dreadful for the Jews who committed them. For them they are gloomy, for us glorious; for them the penalty for killing God, for us the enjoyment of knowing God; for them mourning, for us exultation; theirs is the bloodguilt, ours the benefit. They stand opposed to our gladness, because they dared what was opposed to the Savior who came to them. They rejected him; we received him. They cast the heir out of the vineyard and killed him; we receive the Benefactor within the Church and are given life. They gave a cross; we receive the salvation that comes through the cross. They gave a spear and nails; we receive the immortality that has sprung up through them.

But the sweetest arrow of your passion, Master, strikes me [?] with its own true shot; and enchanted by the ineffable mystery of your saving plan, I am wounded all the more sharply with love for you, who are beyond suffering and yet suffered. Yet my love cannot be set beside your love for us, even if it were kindled to a fiery and unquenchable blaze. For just as a burning heat of nature and the flame of a father's love drive a father on behalf of his beloved children, so it compelled you, who love us as a father, to be so disposed toward us, to descend to such lowliness, and to submit to such sufferings, though you were not liable to them, solely out of tenderness for those you longed for. O the goodness of the Master! God who watches over all things is plotted against; the Son who shares the Father's throne is condemned in the flesh by condemned

men; the King of the heavenly powers is called to account; he who holds all creation in his invisible hand is struck by a most defiled hand; he who is praised by myriads of angels endures mockery and insults; and he who adorned man with a crown of graces is crowned with a crown of thorns. He is scourged who heals the wounds of our nature; he is stripped in his body who as God wraps himself in light as with a garment; he who covered the nakedness that came upon us through transgression, and gave us garments of light in exchange for the dark garment of sin. He hangs upon a cross who fashioned the heights of heaven.
