He who sits on a high and lofty throne is pierced with nails; he who set the earth upon nothing [?] and fixed for it unshakable foundations by his own command. He is given vinegar and gall to drink who brought forth the ever-flowing nature of the waters; the cause of the sweetest qualities, the sweet and unclouded delight. His side is pierced by a spear, he who heals our wounds; who checks the spreading of the sores that grew upon us through sin

But what is this incomparable forbearance of yours, Master, and for whom do you accept these things? For the wicked, you, the good Master, suffer as a man; for enemies and foes, you, the peacemaker; for the bloodguilty, you, the guiltless; for murderers, you, the just Judge, are murdered; for plotting beasts, you, the innocent Lamb, are slaughtered; for bitter judges, you, the sweetest Lord, are condemned. How did the order of the universe keep its proper arrangement then? How were the elements not dissolved and all things thrown into confusion, swept into discord by a disorderly motion? How did the earth endure the outrage? How did it not flee from its seat and give up the whole world to be flooded by the abyss? You, nailed to the wood, held all this back. The earth that was sinking into chaos you raised up [?], and the sea that raged against it and its inhabitants you restrained. So too, when the heavens showed how unbearable the passion was by the darkening of their lights, you did not let them be utterly destroyed; and so too you held back the indignation and righteous wrath of the bodiless ministers. For they broke through the heavens, flew around the place of the Skull, and cried out against humankind: “O wicked creatures! O bloodguilty race, that dared such things against its own Master! O sin-loving nature, raging so against its Creator! Allow us, Master, to bring punishment upon them. Permit them to pay the final penalty for their countless impious deeds. See to what depths of wretchedness they have gone. Against you, their benefactor, they armed their murderous hands; against you, the just one, they wove injustice; against Life they brought the sentence of death, they who are themselves liable to death—this defiled assembly, this utterly hateful tribe!

But yielding to you, who chose these things for their salvation, we are held back by your almighty hand, and so we put off the just penalty; and in amazement we hymn your incomparable forbearance: that you, the just one, suffer for the unjust; that you, the mighty one, are pained in the body for weak enemies; that you, who hold all things together, are held upon a cross by your own will.” So creation, lamenting the passion of the Master, was restrained by the command of the one who suffered, so that it neither rushed against the murderers nor went on to its own dissolution.

But it would be fitting for us to take up the subject at hand and, with its guidance, to hymn the saving passion. For just as it leads us to glorify the whole divine plan, so it will also lead us through this. The passage before us reads: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's sister Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.” The other divine evangelists agree that the women who had come stood far off and watched what was being done; but this one says that the mother and the two Marys stood by the cross itself, and so much nearer that they could hear what was said quietly. Is there then some disagreement among the heralds of the truth? Not at all. For all his acquaintances and the women who followed him were afraid and did not dare to come near, but watched from afar what was being done. But the mother, who always followed more closely, was nearer and would not be moved. For she showed courage and daring in proportion to her burning heart. Seeing her alone holding firm, the two women, braver and more compassionate than the others, came forward, providing her consolation by their presence and their words. This divine theologian, however, mentions only the mother's standing at the cross; neither he nor any other evangelist appears to mention clearly her endurance before and after it. But why they do not show her keeping watch before the cross, we will tell, as those who are ourselves present with Christ at that place, so far as they allow us. When she saw her Son hastening to the saving passion, she could not bear to be parted from him for even the briefest moment. Therefore, following him everywhere, she was not left behind from the [?] of the mysteries [?] (John 19:25).

For when he was hastening to hand down the mysteries and the examples of exalting humility to the disciples, he reclined at table with the twelve alone; but to his mother he gave the care and leadership of the women who ministered to him, and through her he repaid them the kindness of sharing his own meal. For the heralds of the gospel say that there were many women who followed him in each place for the sake of ministering, and these he had to gather together at that time, when it was the matter of the Passover and the need of the hour. So we suppose that she was not absent that night either, on which he was handed over to the saving slaughter; rather, she was present and shared in the struggles, or rather took far more of them upon herself than the others did, and saw and heard more clearly the things that were done and said. For all the disciples were scattered at once by fear and did not clearly grasp even his discourse to those who had gathered with him; but she, shrinking from nothing, followed and watched over the safety [?] of all. For her longing for her dearest one prevailed over the extremity of the dangers before her. So she also went to the court of Annas and Caiaphas, and by searching out each thing she learned of the unjust judgment by those who were themselves condemned and of every outrage they dared. But who could count the things that were then [?] against [?] … [?] … she was untroubled by struggle and higher than the passions of nature, except that her fervent love for her beloved, the excess of the impieties, and the madness of the bold were the cause of unbearable grief for her. How, when he repaid the kindness of his own meal, [?] …

…how did she endure it, to see her all-good Son and Master seized by wicked servants, the meek and innocent Lamb held fast by wild beasts? He spoke to them in a gentle and kindly voice, while those senseless men roared at him with frenzied and savage shouts. What was she then, as she followed him being led away, and when he was brought inside, and as she waited patiently while he was on trial? How she watched the doors for those coming out, and hung on everyone's lips to learn what they might report about the verdict! And when she saw them all alike breathing murder against him, her anguish grew all the more. For there was no one there then to speak up for the truth, no one to denounce the injustice, cry out against the outrage, and so lighten her grief. The whole council was bent on bloodshed; the whole of it breathed out the lawless sentence; not one man sided with a just judgment. His true disciples had fled; others hid the truth out of fear; and the chief of the disciples and friends was denying him. So she alone stood firm and held out through these terrors. She questioned the more reasonable of those coming out of the court, as though she simply wanted to learn the charge and the sentence passed on the righteous man now condemned: "Tell me, sirs, why has this stranger been arrested? What pretext has been stirred up against him, that he is now held and called to account like a condemned man? What vote condemns him? What do the judges think of him? What sentence are they passing on him? Is anyone advising pardon, or have they all brought in a merciless severity?" With such questions she asked, not in a manner unworthy of herself, so that she would not be found out, and yet with deep feeling. She betrayed the flame kindled within her, which had the mastery of her: on the one side it forced its way out into the open, on the other she held it back by force behind an unsuspicious manner. It was not that she refused to [?] on behalf of such a one, but that she was careful to do nothing against the will of the sufferer. And since she was compelled to follow him as he was sent on to Pilate and to Herod, how did she bear to see him dragged about like a criminal? With what soul did she endure to see him now publicly condemned and scourged, now handed over to the soldiers, suffering countless outrages and mocked? How did that life-giving face receive the profane spittle of the unholy? How did she endure to see the eyes that behold all things blindfolded? For this is what being "buffeted" means. Others struck his cheek and his all-holy head in mockery, calling out, "Prophesy to us, Christ!" How did she bear to see that head which she revered, which she kissed and worshipped as the head of her Creator and her Son,

crowned with a crown of thorns and beaten with a reed? How did she bear to see his limbs, so precious and so dear to her, shamefully stripped and then dressed in the mock purple? All this dealt her countless deathblows. Even before the Master's death, each of these things drove a deadly arrow into her, and so in truth it was. But she was upheld by the power of the one who suffered. Who could conceive the burning in her heart when she endured to watch her Son going to his voluntary slaughter? How the Lamb of God was led like an innocent lamb; how he who takes away the sin of the world was dragged off like a condemned man; how meekly he bore the insolence of the murderers; how mild was his bearing toward them; how sweet the look he turned on them; how gentle the words he spoke to them; how calmly he accepted carrying his own cross on his shoulders. For it is written that before they met Simon of Cyrene, those who were hurrying him along laid it on him. And so the tears of the women who followed and beat their breasts chafed her pain more fiercely. Or rather, not their tears, but his own most gentle word to them, as he urged, "Do not weep for me, daughters of Jerusalem." How her heart was torn to pieces at that voice! How her whole being was shaken! How the flame within her was fanned past all bearing! For who, hearing such words, would not have bent, would not have grown softer than any wax, would not have been moved to pity, however stony and unfeeling he might be? Then the murderers reached the place of the Skull and set eagerly about the life-giving death. They fixed the cross in the ground and stripped him of the clothes he wore. The nails whetted their madness, and with murderous intent they made themselves the steps by which he was raised onto the cross. Then the sharper sword was driven into her; then the arrows of pain were aimed at her. But how did her soul not leave her body? How was it not torn from its bond? How did her eyes endure to watch their own light lifted up on the cross? How did her pupils not flee from the sight of those all-spotless palms freely surrendered to murderous hands? How did her joints not fall apart when the limbs of him who holds all things together were being nailed? Oh, the nail was in his hand, but the mortal wound was driven into her heart! How at the piercing of each of his limbs her soul was wounded more painfully still! How drops of blood ran from his wounds, and from her eyes ran streams of tears more bitter! How did she look upon him hanging naked in the body, who in his divinity clothes himself with light as with a garment? How did she bear to see the garments she had made with her own hands, which she had revered as pure because they were worn on the Master's body, divided by lot among foul

and unholy hands? How did she endure to look at his body stretched out on the cross? How did she endure that gaze, so gentle toward her and toward everyone, so meek and forgiving toward the mockers and toward the criminal hanging beside him and reviling him? These things dealt her a painful blow that went deeper than the nails driven into him: I mean the jeers of the passers-by, the taunts of the bystanders, the words of those who gloated and mocked, the sneers, the ironic nods, the countless insults of the murderers. For all of them alike rejoiced in the murder and scoffed. The Prophet, inspired from above, foretold this too when he said, "I waited for someone to grieve with me, and there was no one; and for comforters, and I found none." Then, besides their failure to grieve and to comfort, he shows the excess of their madness and says, "And they gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." And so, struck by countless mortal blows of pain, she strove to draw near and pour out something of her grief, but she was driven back by the soldiers' insolence and by the crowd that surrounded him. But when the God-slayers had done all they wished to dare, and supposed that the killing had come to its end, the crowd went home and the soldiers lay down somewhere nearby to feast. Then, then at last, freed from those who had been jostling her, she came near unhindered, close enough to touch the cross. She kissed the spotless feet and embraced the nail wounds. She gathered the drops of blood and brought them to her eyes and to her heart. Gazing at him and weeping, she spoke to him like this: "What is this, Master? Is this the reward for your ineffable condescension? Is this the repayment for your great compassion? Are these the honours with which those you blessed have repaid you? O most unjust audacity! O unholy judgment! The unjust have condemned you, the just one. The guilty have sentenced the guiltless. The ungrateful kill their benefactor. Wicked servants have hanged their good Master. O foul counsel! O envy raging against my light! O murder armed against my child, born to me without travail! With what audacity have the murderers put to death in the body the life of all,

impassible in his divinity but passible in the flesh by the dispensation? To repay what wrongs have they contrived this unjust murder against you? To exact what just penalty have they staged this dreadful spectacle? Is this how they have repaid your great benefits? Is this the return for countless blessings, and for the gift of coming into being and continuing to exist? For the dead who were raised, they put you to death? For the eyes that were given light, they hurry to close your bodily eyes? For many healings, they have wounded your limbs, so dear to me? For the disfigurement of spotted lepers that you took away, they have stripped you, my sweetest light. They have stripped the Sun of righteousness; they have stripped my most beautiful adornment. They have wounded the limbs of him who kept my purity spotless, who guarded unbroken the seals of my virginity and chastity. Oh, if only I could take your sufferings on myself, my child! If only the nails could be driven into my limbs! If only I had borne the pain of these wounds in my own body! Then perhaps the pain in my heart might be bearable. But now the arrows driven into it are past enduring, and the anguish of my soul is unbearable. For you are the pain of my womb. You, the child who keeps the breath in me, are being killed. You, my only-begotten Child, are being slaughtered. O wicked audacity! Set, O sun, as you see my light, and the light of the world, setting in the body. Shudder, O heaven, and with a gloomy face join in my lament; mourn as you behold the slaughter of the common Master. O earth, foundation of everlasting foundations, mountains and valleys, do not bear this unjust murder quietly. Be shaken, you regions beneath the earth; be downcast with me, all you delights of the meadows. For see, he who adorned you with many-coloured flowers hangs dishonoured on the wood. He who beautified you with countless fragrant hues hangs there without comeliness or form in human eyes: he who is beauty unalloyed, loveliness unchanging, and the unfailing delight of her who bore him. Oh, my sweetest Child! Oh, the one who keeps my soul alive! Now I alone suffer your precious sufferings beyond you; I alone take your pains into my heart more fiercely still. For there is no one to share my anguish, no one to take a part of your bruises with me. Even if some of those present grieve over this murder, it is not as a mother's heart grieves. They are not struck by the goads of nature, nor consumed by the double fire of love, nor bound by those double and most tyrannical bonds. For my bond with a Son who is unchanging and truthful God both draws me and sets me on fire. Beyond nature, then, is the fire kindled in me! The flames that rend me exceed a mother's travail. The sword of your passion goes into my heart more sharply; these pains are more piercing than nature, for the birth too was beyond nature. And the more wondrous that birth was, the more I am wounded, torn

in my inmost being. And it would have been my dearest wish, and easier than the pains that grip me, if the nails had gone into me; if I had received your wounds in my own limbs; if I had been dishonoured by the outrages of countless mockings and scourgings; if a mother's hands had been wounded instead of her dearest child's. But this cannot be, since you alone take on suffering for all. You alone are the Creator, and for this you came. But what shall I do? How shall I bear this dreadful sight? How shall I endure to look at your back, already bloodied with precious blood, and your limbs now reddening? How shall I see those light-giving eyes closed? How shall I behold the tongue and honey-flowing lips that once raised the dead and commanded demons now fall silent, even for a little while? But go, Master, to fulfil this ineffable dispensation. Go, Child desired above every good, to be glorified with the honour that is your due. For I shall no longer embrace you bodily, my [?], because you will raise the nature you have assumed to your divine throne. No longer shall I dress your body with a mother's hands, for you are departing to your own glory, though you were never parted from your first glory. Even if you are present with your mother in a divine way, it will not be as before. It will not be so that I can embrace you, or enjoy the sweet sight of you continually, or delight in your bodily beauty. And yet this is for me the source of the highest glory and joy: through your suffering you have brought about the salvation of all and raised the human clay you assumed to your own throne, and I may be with you spiritually and speak with you always. Yet even so I groan within as I see you in pain and suffering in the flesh, struck by countless insults from those around you and those passing by, and as I see those who ought to have enjoyed your great care thrusting themselves into the pit of destruction. But they are like this by their murderous choice. As for you, speak some farewell word to your Mother, you who are absent from nothing that exists. Speak a sweet and life-giving word, so that I may have it as a comfort for the time to come. Make provision for her who bore you, you who govern her together with your whole world. Speak a word that is sweetest to hear now and firm to hold forever." So the Master saw his own Mother struck by the sharpest arrows of nature. He weighed the fire in her heart and found it equal to what came from her lips, and he let fall the word she longed for. Its power to restore her lay more in its sound than in what it said. For this is what she sought with all her heart: to catch even the bare sound of her dearest one's voice. And his words were such as to show one who settles all things in brief:

"Woman," he says, "behold your son," entrusting her to the disciple. But consider again how the fire of her nature blazed up more fiercely, how the flame within her was fanned past all containing. For by saying "son" he reminded her of that strange and ineffable birth. He reminded her of a love beyond nature, of their beloved days together, of a grief beyond comprehension. He brought to mind the gracious words of a Son to his Mother; his lofty and wondrous obedience; her pride in him; their longed-for and reverent embraces. He reminded her too that she would no longer have the use of such words as before, and that he would no longer spend his days with her continually in the flesh as he once did, for he was hastening to his own glory. "Behold your son." You who have known it in your own lives know how deeply such charges strike home when they are given by those going abroad or by those departing this present life. You know what stirring of the heart they cause, what anguish, what pain. For in place of one who was always loved and always near, people receive one they are not used to. They are told to let go the one who was familiar in every way and was their protector, and to live with one who is a stranger to them in most things. "Behold your son." "You have me," he says, "present with you in my divinity and caring for you as my own Mother. And you have also the beloved disciple, who will fulfil all the duties of sons toward you and pay the debt owed to parents. Look on him in place of my bodily presence, and comfort your unbearable sorrows. Leave off the greater part of your fierce pains. Lighten the heavy grief of nature by the greatness of the blessing. You are cut and burned within, and your heart is wounded beyond measure. For your longing for me is not only natural but beyond nature, and you cannot be made to feel the pain less. Yet you must lessen your grief, since you are my Mother and know the ineffable counsel. For by such sufferings I win impassibility for what I fashioned; by such dishonours I have been pleased to honour the dishonoured race. These outrages are glory beyond all glory for me who suffer in the flesh, and they are the revealing and proclaiming of your greatness. So, since you have the friend who leaned on my breast, cease from your griefs. Live with him and with those around him, and fill my place. For through him I entrust the rest of the disciples to you as well. For as long as I wish you to be with them and to remain in this life, give them your own presence in place of my bodily presence. Be to them all that mothers by nature are to their sons, or rather all that I was when I was with them, and they will be sons and subjects to you. They will pay you fitting reverence as the Mother of their own Master, since it was through you that I came to dwell among them, and in you they have a mediator with me who easily wins reconciliation." So, having spoken kindly to his Mother,

he also gives his charge to the disciple, saying, "Behold your mother." O surpassing honour of the disciple! O inheritance richer than the whole fabric of creation! O grace that the beloved herald received: to be called brother of the Creator of all things, and to receive as his lot and portion of a mother the Lady of all! "Behold your mother." "Behold," he says, "I entrust her to you in my place. Now that I am going to my own glory, I leave her to you in place of my visible self. Fulfil my duty to her as a son, and render her the reverence due to the Mother of your Lord and Teacher. She has me always present with her in my divinity; let her have your unfailing service as well. You by word, and I by deed, will lighten the unbearable weight of her pain. You give her the comfort she is owed, and I will add to it all her endurance. For now I appoint her, as a mother, to be the guide not only of you but of the rest of the disciples too, and I wish her to be honoured properly with the dignity of a Mother. So, although I forbade you to call anyone on earth father, still I wish her to be both honoured and called Mother by you, since she became for me a dwelling above the heavens and showed a choice beyond nature." When the all-good one had made these arrangements with unspeakable patience, the murderous beasts gathered again. They surrounded the cross and drove the much-suffering mother away from where she stood close by and from her converse with him. What contests of martyrs, what severing of limbs, what cutting up of bodies, what devising of instruments of torture could ever have been enough, or reached so deep into the soul, as the countless swords of her Lord and Son's sufferings? These cut her through and stretched her pain beyond all measure. Her soul, cut in so many ways, would not have stayed in her body had it not been held fast by the sufferer himself, had not divine aid worked together with her endurance. Since the mystery of the dispensation was now being fulfilled, and nothing prophesied about him could be left out, the tasting of the gall and vinegar was brought to completion as well, through his confession of thirst. "I thirst," says the Lord. And the Jews had to show such madness. For it was not because of the prophecies, by necessity, that they committed their outrages. Rather, because of their implacable obstinacy the unerring prophecy was both laid down beforehand and fulfilled. But consider how this wound was rubbed into the Mother even more painfully than the pains before it. For no sooner was that cry sent up than her heart was torn apart by it. One could see her running about at his word, cut and burned more fiercely still, looking piteously at the bystanders and begging them all to help her and give her water, so that she could bring it to the mouth of her dearest one and cool the fever of his body; and

she hurried to do it but did not find any at once. Or, having found it, she could not give it to him: either she had no way of reaching him, because his head hung too high and her hand could not get near his mouth, or the murderers pushed her away. They got there first and offered the vinegar, and would not let her treat the hanging man more kindly. Oh, what sufferings the Word met with, sufferings that win impassibility for us but endless punishment for the insolent and disobedient! As for the myrrhed wine, in the excess of their madness they had brought it along with the cross and the nails. For, it says, they offered it to him to drink before he was hung up, and he would not take it. But now they took what was at hand and so gave full vent to the drunken insolence of their own purpose. But what did she suffer… [Note 56: [?] "The myrrhed wine." … [?] having tasted it, he would not drink. (Latin: "When he had tasted it, he would not drink.") … [they gave] him myrrhed wine to drink, but he did not take it … [?]]

…burial, she was considering how it might be done. While she was pondering this and weighing it with the most prudent care, another sword, sharper than the earlier ones, was sent against her: the piercing of the immaculate side. For the soldiers, crueller than any beasts, wounded the life-giving corpse while it still hung there in the body. They did not fear divine justice. Nor were they restrained by nature itself, which feels a common compassion for all who lie dead, even for those who were once enemies and foes. Dead bodies move people so strongly that even those most resistant to pity cannot pass by such a sight without tears. But those stony and unruly men, iron in their inhumanity, felt nothing of our common nature. They saw inanimate creation suffering with him and all but mourning and beating its breast over the saving Passion, yet in an excess of madness and godlessness they assailed the one who hung there and struck him, never sated with their impieties. Having outraged the life-receiving side, they went away from him who consented to make immortality gush forth for us from it in an ever-flowing stream. But the Mother, struck more deeply in her soul, called again and again on him who endured these things, and weeping she spoke thus: “Not even now, Master, do these bloodstained men cease their madness against you; not even now have they had their fill of murder. They are not broken when they see you hanging in such a posture. They are not moved when they behold you nailed up dead and naked. They feel no pity when they see you slaughtered among condemned men and abandoned like an outcast. Instead they assail you with the most savage madness and wound you, my sweetest child; they wound you, who heal the wounds of nature. They pierce the side that pours forth the ever-living stream. They strike without mercy, attacking with deeds and with words, and they do not relent. O bonds and laws and sympathies of nature! O just customs of reverence toward the departed! O ways and marks of human gentleness! Where are these now, and in whom? They have left those who stand here; they have fled from the evil counsel of the God-slayers. But as for me, may the life that drips from the wound be mine and remain with me [?]; and the audacious will see it when they pay the penalty of justice.” Thus, lamenting with compassion and speaking to the Master, she received the blood and water that flowed from the divine side. Having taken it with great longing and the highest reverence,

she turned her care to the burial that would renew all things. She wanted the immaculate body, once taken down from the wood, not to sharpen her pains by remaining in her sight, and she did not want delay in laying it in the tomb to postpone the re-creation of all. She could not accomplish this by herself, because she lacked what was needed: she too was in a foreign place, and her acquaintances stood watching from afar. She also chose not to leave the life-giving body hanging there in order to run about among the wealthy and ask for it. As she pondered this in anguish and considered how a worthy place and a tomb fit to receive God might be found, he who had prepared all things beforehand gave her the means. He put into her mind the thought of searching the ground nearest to Calvary. She judged this a very wise plan, since the work would be accomplished and she would not be deprived of the sight of the all-holy body. Having resolved on this, her feet went off but her soul did not move. Her steps changed place, but her eyes gazed on him without ceasing, unwilling to be parted from that sight even for the briefest moment. When she had searched, she found the tomb suitable, for it was new. The place around it also offered a pleasant and secure view, since at that time it was used as a garden and was beautifully adorned on every side. She asked whose it was, and whether the owner was one of her acquaintances. She learned that the man was a friend, counted among the intimates of the disciples, but still in hiding for fear of the murderers. For so the divine Evangelist says: “but secretly, for fear of the Jews.” She went to him, laid her good counsel before him, and urged him to lay the Life of all in his own tomb, saying: “The murderous deeds of the Jews, Joseph, have come to an end, for the Teacher has accepted them with ineffable long-suffering. They left out no excess of outrage or dishonour; having heaped all these on him, they finally inflicted the shameful death. And now he hangs dead and naked on the wood, a dreadful sight to me and to all creation.

Show kindness, then, to him as your teacher, and to her who bore him, for she is cut by countless pains. Take courage and ask for him. Bring down the body, and gather up the treasure of the world that lies before you. Show kindness to us, who are in a foreign land and in want, hated and shunned by all, loathed and reviled by all, abandoned by acquaintances and friends, pitied by no one. For there is no one to defend us and no one to help. No one dares to ask for the body. No one has made any plan

for these things or seen to the burial. As you see, both of these are impossible for me at present. I stand here alone with only the one disciple. I have no freedom to speak before Pilate, and I have no other means of providing for the burial. We cannot even think how to wrap and cover the nakedness of the one who hangs there. For the soldiers took his garments and divided them, not even leaving the last tunic. This is painful to me and fearful to all insensible creation, but to the murderers it is a cause of delight and of mockery. Come, then, rise above the cowardice and pettiness of everyone else; go and ask for the divine body. Do not fear the fury of the murderers any longer. They have spent all their madness on the one they slaughtered, and with my Light they have brought their plotting to an end for now. This is as far as their daring has gone. Go, then, and hold nothing back. He who suffered willingly will keep you from harm; he himself will go before you as your guide. He will make your words gracious and win them a favourable hearing. For this man, Joseph, though he suffered by his own will as a man, shook the earth as God. He split the rocks, opened the tombs, and drew the dead up from the underworld. Angels were astounded at his Passion; the elements were abashed; the ever-shining lights of heaven shuddered and drew in their rays in fear. You will see these things more clearly as you go out, and you will be stirred [?] more warmly to make your request. There must be no delay or postponement, and no deferring of the re-creation of all. Let the body be laid in the tomb [?], so that it may open the way for the resurrection of mankind.” With such words she taught and urged Joseph, and above all she won him over by her compassionate, motherly bearing. Then she sent him to Pilate. He had not dared to do this on his own so suddenly, nor did he know that the Passion had reached its end, since he was in hiding and very fearful, like the other disciples. But when he learned it from her and was roused by her, he went out more boldly. He made his request and received the Life of all; and having prepared what was needed for the burial, he hurried on the taking down from the cross. But consider, I ask you, how the Mother stood by and persevered, ready for everything. For with the suffering [?] … [the text here is badly corrupted; only fragments can be made out:] … heart … having accepted … of the long-suffering one, his friends and neighbours lamenting … looking upon the one who suffered … of Nicodemus and … and he was there; and comforting …, and he found; and seeing him naked … of the one who buried [?] …

…she spoke [?] with decorum and without faintness of heart, and served the need with her own hands. She received the nails into her bosom as they were drawn out, embraced and kissed the limbs as they were loosed, and took them into her arms; she alone was eager to serve at the descent from the cross. When he had been brought down and the all-holy body laid on the ground, she fell upon it and bathed it in the hottest tears. In a gentle voice and with the most compassionate words she spoke to him, saying: “Behold, Master, the mystery foreordained has been fulfilled. Behold, your loving dispensation has reached its end. Behold, your indescribable forbearance has been set before the eyes of all. For now you, the giver of all breath, lie breathless in the body. I hold and embrace the breathless body of the creator of the life of all, of him who holds my breath in his hand. Breathless now I hold him whom once I embraced as my own most beloved, whose sweetest words I used to hear, in whose life-streaming speech I gloried. I kiss limbs now motionless and wounded, the limbs of him who heals the incurable wounds of nature, who was bruised for the healing of all. I embrace a voiceless mouth and silent lips, the mouth of him who created every rational nature and set man upon the earth as a creature with speech. I kiss closed eyes, the eyes of him who devised the power of sight and by his own command gave light to the eyes of the blind. Oh, that I might hear your sweet voice now! Oh, that I might hear you speak again! Oh, that I might once more catch your longed-for words! But even if that is not possible now, may I soon see it at the resurrection, when you announce the re-creation of mankind and speak more joyfully with her who bore you.” Glorifying him in this way, she adorned the all-immaculate body with divine grave-clothes and a precious linen shroud, giving it a seemly burial. When he had been laid in this tomb that received God, Joseph and Nicodemus and those with them withdrew, while she alone sat before its doors, eagerly awaiting the divine resurrection. But let the account of these things be kept for tomorrow’s splendour. Now it is fitting for me, as I reckon up my thanksgiving, to address you, the Master who suffered for me, who showed unspeakable forbearance and by an unsearchable condescension brought about my ascent from the underworld. I hymn your long-suffering and forbearance, Lord; I hymn your ineffable dispensation; I glorify your surpassing mercy, moved by which you justified me, the condemned. I love your sufferings, through which I

was freed from the most shameful passions. I love your cross, by which you condemned my sin and freed me from the sentence of death. I love those nails, by which you prised away the penalty of the curse. I love the piercings of your limbs, by which the wounds of my disobedience were healed. I love the reed, by which you signed my freedom and wounded the arrogant head of the dragon. I love the sponge brought to your immaculate lips, through which the bitterness of my transgression was turned into sweetness. I would taste the gall as the sweetest food; I would take the vinegar as from a mouth of gladness; I would put on the crown of thorns as a royal diadem; I would adorn myself with the spittings as with shining pearls; I would be glorified by the mockeries as by the highest honours; I would be dignified by the blows as by the most splendid ornament. Loving you, Master, I glory in your sufferings. I love the lance, which tore up the record of my debt and opened the fountain of immortality. I love your side, from which the rivers of life flowed, from which the ever-flowing stream of incorruption gushed forth for me. I love your grave-clothes, by which you adorned me and stripped away the coverings of shame. I love the precious shroud, by which you clothed me in the robe of adoption when you put it on. I love the tomb, in which you renewed the mystery of my resurrection and prepared for me the way up out of Hades. I love that stone, by which you lifted from me the burden of the fear of death. I honour those who served at the life-giving burial, for they obtained so great a grace. I love the hands of her who bore you, for she served your whole divine dispensation: formerly at the birth, and now at the burial, where she alone laboured beyond her strength. Those hands wiped away the precious blood and wrapped the all-immaculate body. I glorify her as the only one seen to share in the saving Passion, as herald of the benefaction, evangelist of immortality, and agent of your shining forth. But, Lady, as you were the first to see him and announce the good news, so may you appear in our hearts, announcing his spiritual dawning, in Christ himself, our sweetest light; for to him belong glory, honour and thanksgiving, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Homily on the immaculate Mother of God’s vigil at the tomb, and in thanksgiving for the most radiant resurrection.

Let a voice of exultation begin our thanksgiving today. Let a voice of gladness sound forth

the thank-offerings for the resurrection of the whole world. Let a voice made splendid to match the present brightness trumpet the doxology. Let it applaud the victory of him who ended the war of the ages, who routed the foe in a war with no truce [?], who through death destroyed the kingdom of death, who bound the strong man and carried off as spoils the souls held from of old. For today his invincible tyranny has been overthrown. Today the King of the heavenly powers has grappled in the flesh with the adversary, thrown him down, and rescued his own creature from harsh slavery. Today he has emptied the fearful, dark storehouses of Hades and brought those who were tyrannized under his own authority. Today the author of our life, having become the firstborn from the dead, has renewed for us the way of immortality. Today heaven has been given to our nature in exchange for the underworld, and to humanity, hidden away in the joyless region, he has assigned the luminous and divine dwelling. Today the most brilliant Sun of Righteousness has cast forth the golden rays of the resurrection and incomparably outshone the beauty of heaven and the adornment of earth. Today, sending forth to the myrrh-bearing women the sweet and most joyful voice of gladness, he has torn out by the roots, rolled up and abolished the sorrows of our race. Come, then, let every tongue that has shared in grace join with me in this praise. Let it come to my aid, for I am overpowered by longing and helpless in speech. For this longing, this is what compels me to touch things beyond nature; this is what drives me toward things beyond my own power; this is what makes me forget my own nature. To yield to it is no dishonour for anyone. For it is a debt, even if it falls short of repayment and is unworthy of the benefits we have received. Yet let it be paid by every rational nature, since the Giver accepts these things in exchange for debts beyond measure [?]. As for me, O divine Love, I am indebted not only for this reason but also because of a promise, which, having been made beforehand, is now demanded like a debt. What this promise is, and of what kind, it is good to add. Already, in what came before, the discourse left the Mother before the door of the life-receiving tomb and reserved what concerned her for today’s brightness. In this way it avoided tedium and kept to the proper order. Now that, by the grace of him who led us here, we have come to the time when the debt is demanded, I hasten to pay it as best I can. The subject calls for skilful treatment: the vigil at the tomb of the Mother of countless trials, for which both the discourse and the debt were undertaken. For she alone, when all had withdrawn, she alone, burning with the fierce fire of her heart [?],

and fixed in unwavering faith and courage, sat there then and persevered, keeping both her eyes sleepless. The divine Matthew does say that the Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting [?] opposite the tomb, but only to watch, since they did not dare to come near even at the time of the burial. So it came about that they also withdrew, for fear of the Jews and because the guard had arrived. Matthew himself confirms this, saying: “After the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.” He would not have said that they came if they had remained there, unless they too, like the rest, had withdrawn. Now some take the one called “the other Mary” to be the one he mentioned earlier [?], and Mark indicates her more clearly when he says: “Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.” Others have supposed her to be the one called the mother of James, whom this same evangelist says is different from the mother of Joses, and the truth confirms it. But I think these are the conjectures of inquirers who do not get to the truth of the matter and who search not from any clear evidence but only from vague and obscure suspicions. For where did they get the idea of inventing such a renaming, when throughout all the divine Gospels we see the Mother, after the ineffable conception, called by this most proper title? “He took,” it says, “the child and his mother.” And: “The mother of Jesus was there.” And again: “His mother said to the servants.” And: “He went down to Capernaum, he and his mother.” And: “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside.” And: “Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister.” And Luke says in Acts: “All these were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of the Lord Jesus.” In short, nowhere can we see her given another name, or called after her father or some family relation, in place of her most particular, honoured and appointed title. There is also firmer testimony on this matter: the most truthful account of the inspired evangelists. For while the beloved disciple said that she was near the divine cross and almost touching it, the others, by contrast, recorded that these women stood far off and watched what was happening. “There were many women there,” says Matthew, “watching from afar, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and the mother of Joses, [?] [marginal note, garbled: Matt. 27:55; variant readings: “of James and Joses, mother”; “the mother of Joses”]

and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.” Mark and Luke indicate the same women in less specific terms. And although it is written that Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene were with her at the cross, we must believe that they were present for the reason given [?]. So none of the women mentioned, or of those to be named in this passage, is the Mother, the one with many titles. For those women went in and out of the tomb all night long and reported to the apostles what they saw, so that they did not get to see most of the wonders of the resurrection. But she sat opposite the tomb without moving and saw everything more clearly; and she told of it afterwards, not at once. How else could the earthquake, the descent of the angel, the moving of the stone, and also the deathlike stupor of the guards, their waking again, and the departure of some of them to the city all have been seen by women who kept going away and coming back, unless someone was there continually, persevering and keeping a keener watch? In this way, not only on that occasion but from the moment the Master was arrested, she saw more clearly than anyone what took place. She never left him, nor did she give way in the least to the needs of the body—I mean sleep and food—until she rejoiced in his life-bearing rising. For the myrrh-bearing women saw the stone rolled away and the angel sitting on it, but whence and how these things had been done they did not know. Matthew, going beyond what they saw, records what happened before they arrived: the earthquake, the descent of the angel, and the moving of the stone. The other evangelists recounted only the vision of the angels and what the angels said to the women, which is what the women actually experienced. Yet Matthew too shows this very thing by his use of the past tense. “An angel of the Lord,” he says, “came down from heaven, came and rolled away the stone, and sat on it.” The word “sat” indicates the time after the women came, and the other verbs [?] the time before it. So the Mother alone [?] knows what happened before they came, and that sweet and mighty earthquake which woke the dead of ages and put the wakeful guards to sleep. Through this, it seems to me, the good news of the divine resurrection was given to her first, and she was able to delight in the ineffable dispensation and in the sight and splendour of her Son. For since she was his Mother and alone had been entrusted with the mysteries of the dispensation, to her alone the Master also showed the marvels of the resurrection, above the apostles and the myrrh-bearers, and even above what angels and spiritual beings are given to know. So the brightness of the rising shone on her directly and first; on the others

…to the myrrh-bearing women it is not made known in the same way, but through both the angel and the moving of the stone. Because they were in a weaker state, it is revealed to them neither all at once nor in one way only. They receive their faith in it partly through hearing, by the angel's word, and partly through sight, by the rolling away of the stone. So, when they had been led by the hand little by little toward the mystery, he himself appears to them, the Life and the Resurrection. His wisdom and understanding arranged things this way for two reasons. If he had been shown all at once, he might in their astonishment have been taken for a phantom, as indeed some of the disciples suspected. And once he was believed, he might have driven the women who believed into something senseless and uncontrollable through the intensity of their joy. For even with things arranged this way, when he appeared to them they rushed with an unrestrained and uncontrollable impulse and clasped his immaculate feet. Had it not been so arranged, what bounds of decorum would they not have overstepped, overmastered by the vehemence of their joy? This, then, is how the resurrection is revealed to Mary and the women with her. To the Mother, however, it is revealed more mystically and more intimately. [?] This is indeed the most notable and genuine mark of her understanding, which surpasses thought: she did not announce these things in advance, on her own, either to the myrrh-bearers or to the apostles. Rather, she allowed them to become eyewitnesses and so to hold the truth more firmly. For throughout the whole dispensation she conducted herself with perfect wisdom. She did not give out on her own what she knew beforehand. Instead she asked it of God and, as mediator, gave it to those to whom it belonged. The heralds knew, then, that the Mother had been the first to be initiated, and more clearly than anyone, into the divine raising, and that through her the myrrh-bearers too had their greater assurance [?]. Yet they chose not to mention her at all in their accounts of that event. In this they were evidently guided by fitting wisdom and by the forethought of the Spirit. Had they brought her forward as a witness in her own cause, she would have been suspected of securing glory for her own, and they would have given unbelievers grounds to think the testimony suspect. And so they fittingly pass over here what concerns her. But I would say it is entirely fitting for the present festival if we now take up the words of thanksgiving she offered as she sat there, and join in them. For she spent the time before the resurrection in stillness. She pondered the marvel, meditated on the mystery, and conversed alone with him who was fulfilling the awesome dispensation. In quiet, and in her own voice, she went over words such as these: "You, Lord," she says, "who possess the impassible and indestructible [?] (To those with Mary: Magdalene.)

nature of the Godhead, suffered as a man in the nature you assumed. You," she says, "without being parted from the Father's bosom, dwell in the hollows of the earth. You are uncircumscribed in the universe as God, yet you are bodily enclosed in a tomb. So the souls of the righteous dance as they receive you. With such voices they greet you, their Redeemer. So, lit by your ineffable radiance, they proclaim your unspeakable love for mankind. But show the trophies of the war to those in the world as well. [?] you who are invisibly present, with fitting beauty. Make the splendor of the resurrection shine to the ends of the earth. Rise in the body, you who as God cannot be held. Awake, then, you who never sleep through all the ages. Awake, to be [?] by the assemblies of the peoples who sing your praise. Awake to defend your poor, and to scatter the opposing powers to their utter destruction. Show the rays of the resurrection, O Sun of righteousness. Let the lightnings of victory shine upon the world. Let these saving deeds be made known to all. Let the poor see and be glad. May I too see the longed-for sight of my most longed-for Master. May I see the surpassing beauty of a Son beyond nature. May I behold the glory of God dawning in him, glorified. May I hear a divine voice uttering sweet and gracious words. As you appeared first to your mother at your coming, so appear now too, bringing the good news of the joy of your raising. Appear, you who are always with her and keep her unvanquished." So it is to the Virgin, theologian and myrrh-bearer, as she sang his praise and made supplication, that the Son first shows the brightness of the resurrection. She had already been pierced by swords, as far as that was possible,

and had shared in her Son's sorrows, and so she alone was granted to enjoy that divine delight beforehand. But what mind could conceive the glory, O Master, that she received from you? What intellectual nature could grasp your inconceivable beauties, which you then revealed to her as to a Mother? O with what radiance you appeared to her! With what love you then made all creation shine! In what light-filled vision you were seen by those in the world! What fragrance breathed through all things from that sweet earthquake, which became the herald of the resurrection! What perfumes the earth gave forth when you, the inexhaustible myrrh, overflowed! O how the whole ordered world was then transformed into newness! How the elements were refashioned into a finer harmony! How the air was adorned with calm and with sweet breezes! What beauties rose from the choir of the stars! How much brighter shone the shafts of the sun's rays! What delight there was in the heavenly order! What a choir of angels was gathered! How sweet was the sound of their doxology! O with what divine splendors they were then adorned! What radiance clothed the heralds of your raising! What glory and beauty they showed to those who saw them! O those voices and words that announced victory over the enemy, that proclaimed the destruction of death, that brought those on earth the good news of you, the Life and the Resurrection! O your voice, sweet beyond everything desired, which sounded joy to the world through the myrrh-bearers, which broke the grievous bonds of sin, which made gladness dwell in the ears of all! For it was fitting that Joy itself and Delight should open the calling of mankind with such a proclamation, and address those held under sin's grievous penalty with so joyful a greeting. It was fitting that such good news should run ahead of your coming and of your benefaction. All creation leapt for joy. Then the heavens spread open their gates and received the message from those on earth as their own. The [?] powers exulted and, rejoicing in human delight, struck up a shared and most joyful dance. Then both the intelligible and the sensible world were lit up. The clouds of despondency were driven from the ends of the earth, and rays of good cheer embraced all things. Condemned nature put off its gloom and put on the robe of light. The bond of the curse was torn up, and promises of blessing were written in its place. Through the life-giving greeting "Rejoice!" all things were filled with your sweetest and unending joy. For you are the exultation of gladness [?], its herald and its cause, maker of good things and giver of delight, life and resurrection, an adornment that cannot be taken away. You are sweet light and a sight longed for above all, calm perceived by the mind and peace that has come,

wisdom itself and power and giver of understanding, incorruption and [?], permanence and delight, abiding and unchanging beauty, [?] beyond thought, resourceful comeliness, holiness itself and honor and righteousness, and glory glorified beyond all glory. You alone are undiminished longing and irrepressible desire, a beauty at once nameless and many-named and desirable above all desire. O how many names the mind labors to bring forth [?] to match your unspeakable beauty! But it is held back by its own weakness and by the poverty of the tongue. But you are a good of ten thousand names and yet beyond naming, raised above every power to invent titles. You attend not to words but to the ardor of the will, and you come to announce to us the joy that you announced beforehand through the myrrh-bearers. Let the brightest light of your appearing shine on us now as well. May we see with the mind the surpassing beauty of the spiritual Sun. May we feast with longing on the most desirable sight of the Master. May we hear a divine voice calling out a sweet and joyful proclamation, and may we receive the most gladdening tidings of your kindness. May we have a myrrh-bearer through whom you may announce to us the joy that cannot be taken away, and through whom you may convey to us the fragrance of your benefits. It is she who brought the inexhaustible myrrh, and she who both procured for us and proclaimed you, our exultation, our life and resurrection. You smelled in her the fragrance of purity, beyond all perfume, and you made your dwelling in her, and through her you came to dwell among us. Through her, then, lover of good, you proclaimed beforehand the coming of your joy-bringing reconciliation. Come, to rescue us from present things as from the lowest depths. Prepare the way for us to unaging life, and number us among the choirs on high of those who keep the feast. For you are light and life and resurrection, and the delight of those who rejoice in heaven. To you belong glory, honor and worship, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

Encomium on the holy wonder-working Unmercenaries, Cosmas and Damian. When I look at your zeal for piety, O lover of good things, I cannot help marveling. But when I consider the weight of your command, astonishment and trembling win out. For to such a height

of love for God have you gratefully risen that you long to attain the greatest things, and you summon many to take up their boundless praise. But we must not let the extraordinary demand of the one who commands us make us fall short of his devout purpose. We must instead show a willing mind. Even if we fall entirely short of words worthy of the present subject, we should at least not fall short of the eagerness of the one who proposed it. For our own eagerness too has its ardor, kindled by love of the good. Yet it is held in check. Its flame is broken up as if by some damp fuel, and the greatness of the subject, overwhelming and beyond our power, blocks its passage. Still, it seizes on some opening and tries most earnestly to bring out into the open an abundance of words [?].

You, then, excellent friend, who spur me on to praise these men, will perhaps look for the usual amplifications of encomia [?], and demand that they be raised high with some showy elaboration. But if occasions for praise are offered, these men will reject both the things themselves and the solemn phrases devised from them. What gave them no pleasure when it lay before them, they will resent seeing displayed in words. And how could they fail to rebuke, and rightly, those who try to glorify them with the goods of their homeland, when they themselves were hostile to its overflowing wealth, its abundance and its great possessions? They will say, and very fittingly, mocking such efforts and cutting short the zeal of those who make them: "Let no one, by ranking first in words the visible pleasures that we renounced, insult the grandeur of the spiritual goods that we ranked first in deeds. And let no one who plans this think that he adds a solemn ornament to our supposed renown by means of the very things we cast away in order to gain glory that lasts forever. For we counted them a loss, not a gain, to what we desire, and we reject the boasts that come from them. To us the splendor of cities and buildings counted for nothing. So did land so fertile that it is weighed down with fruit in season, and the delights of many-colored meadows. So did regions blessed with mild air, and springs that open in the clearest streams and give the greatest pleasure to the eye before the taste. So did rivers that run down from the mountain ridges and gently pour their waters into valleys and plains, making them green and full of flowers, and that by the smoothness of the season draw onlookers to them with pleasure. In the same way the abundance brought in by sea is despised through a wealth of owning nothing. Gold, which enslaves souls, is trampled underfoot. Its tyranny, which overpowers others, drags its captives to itself almost like slaves and subjects them, has been defeated."

Such are the things those who regard the delights of apparent goods in this way will say, with reasonable frankness, or even with authority. But you, admirable friend, will have us pass over these too, and after giving brief attention to describing them, you will urge our narrative on toward the portrait of their parents. And that is well advised. For those who shared in good things, or rather who themselves became the source of them, ought also to share in the glory of praise. They had the good fortune to be genuine kin both by nature and in deeds, and so, quite reasonably, they should not be shut out from sharing in the good fortune of these words. Those whom character joined, the speech of praise does not separate. The saints who are the occasion of our praise display the renown of the father from whom they sprang. For the training by which they ascended to the height of virtue and were deemed worthy to approach God, who is exalted above all, proclaims those who guided them [?], and bears witness that their parents fittingly share in their goods. The father of the far-famed Unmercenaries, then, set them on the path of godly conduct and of the most venerable life, left it to their mother to guide them to completion, and departed to the heavenly dwellings. She took up the fulfilment of words given as charges [?] and of hopes still uncertain, and by constant care she brought about in the children left to her what had been hoped for. For she was Theodote, "given by God," and she sealed her name with deeds and confirmed its glory by the facts themselves. She had risen above earthly things and was lifted higher than nature, passing over not with visible wings but by purity and reason.

Theodote was a gift given by God, but she gave back to the Giver, together with herself, the fruit of her womb as well. She brought him a twofold offering and in this outdid Abraham. She brought a whole sacrifice to the one sacrificed [?] for mankind, and was deemed worthy of a better acceptance than Abraham's. She did not sharpen a knife for it, build an altar, gather kindling or light a fire, nor did she foul the air with smoke and the reek of fat. Instead, she held over those she offered, as a knife, the self-control that cuts away the passions. She raised up an altar of teaching, the most pure dwelling of their soul, and in it fire kindled from divine longing completed the sacrifice and bore it up, fragrant and most acceptable, to the Beloved. Having thus rightly divided her own offering, she arranged that it should be rightly offered up by the free choice of those being offered. For she sowed the seeds of good things in her children, and they chose to bear abundant fruit from what was sown,

[?] and what they judged good, they carried into action. They preferred love of God to every other desirable thing. They kept their faith unadulterated and constantly bore the witness of their conscience. They were bound by unbreakable love to their neighbors. They broke away from passionate pleasures and showed courage against them. They put to death the members of the body and strengthened the powers of the soul. And by the zeal with which they achieved the greatest things in the prime of youth, they foreshadowed the newness of the gifts that were to be theirs, which would proclaim the marvel not only by the greatness of what they would accomplish but by its sheer number. So Cosmas and Damian, watered and nourished by the achievements of their youth like noble saplings, shot up to a boundless height of virtues and gifts. Cosmas and Damian adorned their souls with godly deeds and, adorned by these, became adorners of the whole world through the many-lighted brilliance of their miracles. They adorned the minds of men with words of piety, and they were given as an adornment to bodies by chasing away unseemly diseases. In the most perfect virtue and practice, then, they received by a more divine inspiration a sure and unadulterated judgment, and they loathed love of money, the cause of everything contrary and the enemy of good things. They had been taught by the words of the divine Paul and learned by experience that it truly is the root of the whole catalogue of evils. Because of it strife and battles and implacable wars are stirred up. Because of it even closely related families make war on one another; father resents son, and child plots treacherously against father. For love of it brothers dissolve the bond of nature and devise worse things against it than enemies would. Because of it uprisings are prepared not only of foreign nations but of neighboring ones. Because of it the most savage tyrannies are sharpened like swords and hurled against a well-governed and pious empire that holds its power from God. Because of it men dare the murder of their own kin and the utter destruction of peoples. Through it the hands of the unjust prevail, murder swells, greed overflows, and poverty and want strangle those who are defrauded. Whoever luxuriates in it with pleasure is wholly cut off from delight in what is truly good, and is rich only in the opposite. He is dragged toward pleasures and behaves like a madman toward his neighbors. He raises his eyebrows and looks about him arrogantly. He thinks great and senseless thoughts. He is all but ignorant not only of the lowliness of his nature and the dissolution of the body, but also of the punishments that await him and the inexorable sentence of a just Judge. And even so, absorbed in his love of money and so disposed toward his neighbors and toward his own salvation, he lives a life harder than that of wretched slaves,

subject and enslaved to it, not allowed even to breathe freely. For its sake he consents to toil and wear himself out and to take on countless cares. He spends sleepless nights scheming over its increase and its growth through trade, and contriving sales and exchanges of goods that are plentiful elsewhere. He asks how much wine is selling for, how much livestock, or wool. Sometimes he lets his thoughts run even to hay, and imagines exchanging it for gold. Then he ponders even more laboriously what trade among his schemes would cost him nothing, who would guarantee it, and who would be a fit partner for merchandise that carries no loss. And if in his anxiety he happens to fall into a very light and unpleasant sleep, he dreams of collecting gold and storing it in purses. Waking takes it away from the hand that seemed to hold it, and through his disappointment drives into him, like an arrow, a grief that is real. Such are his nightly fancies and musings. As for the miseries of his day, I mean the laying of a Spartan table, a self-imposed scarcity of food, the starving of his servants, and the driving away of the poor who beg from him, not only without kindness but with insults and blows, he himself could perhaps describe them as they deserve, or show them by his very deeds, putting his own wickedness on display. As for us, though we would gladly depict this as well as we can in a set exercise, the subject in hand bids us lead our discourse, which runs off like a colt, around its own turning-post and steer it to its proper course. It will follow that course without delay in what comes next. The Unmercenaries, then, lovers of truth and merchants of golden virtue, knew full well that love of money enslaves the nature of greedy men. So they pulled it up by the roots from their own souls, and pulled up with it the swarm of evils: irrational desire, beastly anger, the tyranny of pleasures. They cut down the puffed-up pride of vainglory, the attachment of self-love, the injustice of greed, the mad swelling of arrogance and the hardness of mercilessness. Those branches had grown up and sprouted alongside the root of evils and were cut away with it. In their place, by grafting in freedom from love of money, they made the noble shoots of owning nothing spring up together: a way of life equal to the angels', a life that blossoms with purity, [?] self-control, holiness, humility the mother of gentleness, love that gives birth to compassion, an inexhaustible spring of mercy. And love, through which they imitated Christ's love for mankind and received from him the grace of working wonders. For they yoked this love to their freedom from money, or rather to their total poverty, and fashioned, as it were, a fiery chariot; and driving a strange kind of chariot-course

…[?] they drew near to God, as far as created beings can, by a kind of spiritual intimacy, and they enjoyed his gifts beyond all thought. For they longed for him alone and never grew sated, and they loved their neighbours more than themselves, or, to put it better, as themselves, and so succeeded in showing their love for him by their very deeds. From this the floodgates of heavenly graces were opened to them. From this an abyss of good things was poured out on them. In this way the wealth of the better gifts abounded for them: a wealth that poverty brought to birth, that having no possessions gathered, that refusing money adorned, that contempt for present things stored up, that longing for God increased, and that love for their fellow men amassed. This wealth, which abounded in the eyewitnesses and servants of God the Word, overflowed its bounds into those who became like them in deeds and in word. For they courageously took over the apostles' contests: the labours for the truth; the journeys; the concern for the health of souls; the care for the healing of bodies; the zeal that cost nothing; the courses run without pay; a life not only free of excess but wholly in want, like the life of the needy; the stripping away of present things; the crucified life. Through this life they became sharers in the resurrection of the one who suffered, and from him who rose and raised the dead with himself they received the power to rekindle human hopes that had been deadened by overwhelming suffering. What speech could recount their deeds as their greatness and number deserve? What speech could touch their majesty even in some small degree? How many tongues would it take? Not even ten thousand, nor many times that number. Not even as many tongues as there are people living now could say anything fitting if they tried to describe them. For these things are honoured beyond expression, and beyond thought as well. Since they are wonders of the incomprehensible God, they are glorified beyond interpretation. Since they are gifts wondrously renewed, they decree that they be marvelled at beyond utterance. Reasoning cannot conceive them, and speech cannot display them. They fall under no measure and are bounded by no time. For they are accomplished continually and every day, so that they stretch the count to infinity and become a prize contested between the two ages. The past contends for them. It puts forward the new wonders already wrought within it and shows that their flow is beyond counting. By its good fortune, it claims, it deserves to be marvelled at more than the age after it, and the antiquity of the deeds should win it reverence. The present contends in return. It claims both that it has the advantage in what was established earlier and that it is honoured for the incomparable wonders newly wrought. The past prides itself on displaying its wonders in written records [?]. The present, together with the records that keep memory alive in the same way, takes pride in setting forth also the recent wonders, which are more plainly in view.

Yet though both think highly of themselves, both alike fall short in counting the wonders that have been worked. For just as these things cannot be conceived or expressed in speech, so they cannot be confined by time. For which of you, O stewards of extraordinary wonders, could any span of time or any reasoning suffice to marvel at your miracles? Still less could anyone write down or tell in articulate speech the wonders worked in your visitations of souls: the quenching of burning passions; the calming of savage and surging passions; the battle line against spiritual enemies; the routing of visible ones; the guarding of chastity. In the same way your varied visitation of bodies displays manifold benefactions. In this way the Lord, who alone is most wonderful, has made his own power wonderful in you. For "in his saints," says the Psalmist, "he has made wonderful." He did not say "he was made wonderful," but "he has made wonderful." For God is wonderful by nature, he means, and needs no addition of miracles in order to be made wonderful. But in the saints he makes his own benefactions wonderful; he makes wonderful the portents accomplished through them; he makes wonderful his own strength in them, and the marvels newly wrought through them. And the Psalmist sets out quite clearly why God makes them wonderful. What is the reason, and of what kind is it? "For all his wishes," he says, "are in them." God makes his gifts wonderful in those in whom his wishes are fulfilled; in whom his commands are carried out with unhesitating resolve; in whom faith is kept unadulterated and the saving laws are observed; in whom he and the Father come and make their dwelling, once they have first been purified and sanctified by the coming of the Holy Spirit. So in you it is clearly shown, through the rewards, that his commands have been fulfilled, and fulfilled to the full extent that the rewards demonstrate in fact. For these things are gifts and are honoured as gifts. But they are measured out and granted according to the zeal and choice of those who draw them down and receive them worthily. Therefore the abundant sharing of these gifts makes plain your God-loving choice, you who received them, and the preparation through works that matched it, and sets them forth in action for anyone who wishes to examine them. For who, whether among those of today or those of the most ancient times, has been so enriched with the grace of miracles that, if he were set beside your gifts, the greatness of his virtue would not fall short [reading "ὑφίεται"]? Abraham the just was celebrated as preferred above everyone in his time. Yet he will be seen to fall short in most of your graces, through which your most holy life and surpassing virtue show that you are beyond compare. For he loved the God of all, but you loved him exceedingly,

having taken up for his sake a bodiless and angelic way of life. He offered to God as a sacrifice the fruit of his loins, in obedience to the command of the one who received it. But you offered your bodies of your own accord, burning them as a whole offering with the sword of divine longing and the fire of self-control. He received a ram as a ransom for the one being offered. But you made the offering and prevailed [?], and needed no substitute. He offered once. But you were offered throughout your whole life, crucified and put to death to the world, and dying all through your life. He is admired for his hospitality, and indeed the deed deserves wonder and is true to his greatness of soul. But his hospitality was poured out from the abundance of his possessions and given to whoever happened to pass by. You, however, placed yourselves in the rank of those who receive hospitality, in a poverty that was voluntary and not unwilled, and you entertained all the needy with a better hospitality. You welcomed them and strengthened them in soul and body. You spread your hospitality not in one time or one place but everywhere on land and sea. You nourished them spiritually. You restored the wasted in bodily ways, and turned their loss of appetite into fullness by giving them a desire for food. He once entertained, in the guise of angels, the Godhead that is not circumscribed by nature, which prefigured the one of the Trinity who would be seen among men. But you enjoyed its illumination throughout your whole life and were called lights of the world. You displayed its unfailing beneficence in wondrous healings. And not only when you were present, but also now that you have departed, you reveal its abundant gifts through your deeds, speaking of God in purity and drawing it into working with you. Yet why must we compare those born of the patriarch, or the righteous who came after them, with you and the gifts given you by God, when the patriarch himself suffices for the comparison? He suffers no diminishing of his own virtue by it. Rather, the comparison shows that the gift granted by grace is beyond compare and without limit, as is shown through words and through the deeds themselves. Indeed, you became imitators of the servants and heralds of this grace, and so you enjoyed gifts equal to theirs. For those whose contests are equal receive gifts in equal measure. Walking in their footsteps, you took on the labours of the saving preaching and did not fall short of running a course equal to theirs. You anointed people's souls toward piety with your words. You rooted out the sowings of tares. You planted the pure doctrines of theology. You practised a life without possessions. You were rich in the gifts of the Spirit. You took up arms against the many sufferings of bodies, and fought and routed their countless afflictions. Freely the [?]

For you had received the benefactions of the Giver and obtained his wealth as a free gift, and you considered the love for mankind of the one who supplied it and the grace that befitted apostles. So it was fitting for you to imitate the Benefactor through your care for those who receive benefit. For you serve them not for your own glory but for his, and you make sure that the greatness of the gift is proclaimed. For he gave to the eyewitnesses and initiates, says the divine evangelist, "authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out." So what was given to them by promise has been granted to you through the outcomes themselves. Authority over unclean spirits has been given to you, so that they do not merely shudder at you as God's servants, and fear and tremble. They are also driven out and routed, and find no place to lodge. "And to heal every disease," he says. He does not mean that you should heal one disease because it is easy to cure and pass by another because it looks difficult. By saying "every," even of those thought incurable, he has given you a power of healing that works with the greatest ease. This holds even if a disease happens to be chronic and has been given up by those who study such things and seem to judge from what they see how things will turn out, and even if it looks toward death itself. For such is the truthfulness of the promise. So by saying "every," and by adding no distinction among the diseases that would be healed, he indicated also those that look toward the end. He showed that you have received the boldness, through your supplications to Christ, to rescue us even from deadly sufferings and diseases. Since, then, you received this from him, and since by imitating the Giver's love for mankind you can do good to the needy without toil, be moved now by the pleas of those in need. Hear the words sent up from the depths of the heart. Give ear to anguished groans. You have the abundance of healings that you received from above. You also have the ability, without toil, to give them to those who ask, unless some obstacle shuts those who ask out from the grace. The obstacle to the benefaction is sin. It gives birth to the worst of afflictions and causes their pains to drag on a long time, but it is defeated and dissolved by your most steadfast intercessions. So do not attend to its opposition and allow your ever-flowing grace to be held back on a just ground.
